children.name: Decapoda
Cambaridae
Faxonius
children.description: Faxonius is a genus of freshwater crayfish that includes many of New England's most common crayfish species. These crustaceans are bottom-dwellers that live in streams, rivers, ponds, and lakes throughout the region, where they serve as both predators and prey in aquatic ecosystems. All members of this genus have the typical crayfish body plan with a hard exoskeleton, large claws, and a segmented tail.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Faxonius crayfish are distinguished from other crayfish genera by specific arrangements of spines and ridges on their shells, particularly around the head region called the carapace. They also have characteristic differences in their reproductive structures that help scientists identify them.
children.funFact: The Quinebaug River Crayfish is found only in a small area of Connecticut and Massachusetts, making it one of New England's rarest crayfish species with an extremely limited range.

children.name: Procambarus
children.description: Procambarus is a genus of freshwater crayfish that includes some of the most familiar and widespread species in North America. These aquatic crustaceans are characterized by their robust bodies, powerful claws, and ability to thrive in various freshwater habitats from streams and rivers to ponds and wetlands.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Procambarus are distinguished from other crayfish genera by their specific body proportions, claw shape, and reproductive structures. They typically have relatively broad, flattened bodies and well-developed chelae (claws) compared to many other crayfish groups.
children.funFact: The Red Swamp Crayfish (Procambarus clarkii) is one of the most widely distributed crayfish species in the world and has become an important food source in cuisines from Louisiana to China, where it was introduced for aquaculture.

children.name: Cambarus
children.description: Cambarus is a genus of freshwater crayfish that are native to eastern North America. These small lobster-like crustaceans live in streams, rivers, and lakes throughout New England, where they play important roles as both predators and prey in aquatic ecosystems. They are characterized by their hard exoskeletons, large claws, and ability to walk backwards when threatened.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of the Cambarus genus are distinguished from other crayfish by their specific gill and reproductive structures, as well as their preference for cooler, well-oxygenated waters. They typically have more robust claws and shorter, stockier bodies compared to some other crayfish genera.
children.funFact: Cambarus crayfish can regenerate lost claws and legs, growing back these body parts over several molting cycles if they lose them while escaping predators or during fights with other crayfish.

children.description: Cambarid crayfishes are freshwater crustaceans that look like miniature lobsters, with large claws, segmented bodies, and long antennae. They live in streams, ponds, and lakes throughout New England, where they scavenge for food on muddy and rocky bottoms. These fascinating creatures play important roles in freshwater ecosystems as both predators and prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike marine lobsters, cambarid crayfishes live exclusively in freshwater and are much smaller, typically measuring 2-6 inches long. They can be distinguished from other crayfish families by specific gill structures and the arrangement of their body segments.
children.funFact: Many cambarid crayfishes are ecosystem engineers that dig elaborate burrows in stream banks and pond edges, creating important habitat for other small aquatic animals.

children.name: Portunidae
Callinectes
children.description: Blue crabs are swimming crabs with distinctive blue-tinged claws and legs, though their shell colors can vary from blue-green to brown. These crabs are excellent swimmers thanks to their paddle-shaped back legs, and they're well-adapted to life in brackish waters where rivers meet the sea.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Blue crabs can be identified by their broad, somewhat flattened shells with sharp spines along the edges and their powerful swimming legs that look like paddles.
children.funFact: Blue crabs are amazing travelers - they can swim backwards, sideways, and forward, and some individuals migrate over 100 miles between feeding and breeding areas!

children.name: Achelous
children.description: Achelous is a genus of swimming crabs that are well-adapted for life in sandy and muddy coastal waters. These crabs have flattened, paddle-like back legs that help them swim efficiently through the water column and bury themselves in soft sediments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other crab genera, Achelous crabs have distinctly flattened rear legs modified into swimming paddles, and their carapace (shell) is relatively wide and streamlined for swimming.
children.funFact: These crabs are sometimes called 'portunid crabs' and can actually swim backwards by rapidly flapping their paddle-shaped legs, allowing them to quickly escape predators.

children.name: Arenaeus
children.description: Arenaeus is a genus of swimming crabs known for their flattened, paddle-like hind legs that make them excellent swimmers in marine waters. These crabs have broad, somewhat rounded shells and are typically found in sandy or muddy coastal environments where they can bury themselves for protection.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other crabs, Arenaeus crabs have distinctly flattened rear legs shaped like paddles, which allow them to swim effectively through the water column rather than just walking along the bottom.
children.funFact: The speckled swimming crab can actually swim backwards using its paddle-shaped legs, often doing so when trying to escape predators or when startled by divers.

children.name: Portunus
children.description: Portunus is a genus of swimming crabs known for their exceptional aquatic abilities and streamlined bodies. These crabs have specially modified paddle-like hind legs that make them powerful swimmers, unlike many other crab species that primarily crawl along the bottom. They are active predators that can chase down prey both on the seafloor and while swimming through the water column.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Portunus crabs are distinguished by their flattened, paddle-shaped rear legs (called swimming paddles) and their relatively narrow, streamlined carapace compared to other crab genera. Their body shape and specialized limbs are specifically adapted for fast swimming rather than just bottom-dwelling.
children.funFact: Portunus crabs can swim backwards, forwards, and sideways with equal ease, making them some of the most agile swimmers in the crab world.

children.description: Swimming crabs are a family of crabs specially adapted for life in the water, with flattened, paddle-shaped back legs that work like oars to propel them through the water. Unlike most crabs that crawl along the bottom, these athletic crustaceans are excellent swimmers that can dart quickly through the water column to catch prey or escape predators. They're commonly found in coastal waters, estuaries, and sandy or muddy bottoms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Swimming crabs can be identified by their distinctive flattened rear legs (called swimming paddles) and typically wider, more streamlined shells compared to other crab families. Their last pair of legs are modified into broad, flat appendages that look quite different from the pointed walking legs of most other crabs.
children.funFact: Blue crabs can swim backwards, forwards, and sideways at speeds up to 3.4 miles per hour – making them some of the fastest swimmers in the crab world!

children.name: Palaemonidae
Palaemon
children.description: Glass shrimps are small, translucent crustaceans that get their name from their nearly transparent bodies that allow you to see their internal organs. These delicate-looking shrimp are commonly found in shallow coastal waters, tide pools, salt marshes, and estuaries throughout New England. They play important roles as both predators of small organisms and prey for fish and birds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Glass shrimps can be identified by their clear, glass-like bodies and long, thin rostrum (pointed beak-like projection) that extends forward from their head. Unlike many other small shrimp, they have relatively large eyes and long antennae that can be longer than their body.
children.funFact: Despite their fragile appearance, glass shrimps are excellent jumpers and can leap several times their body length to escape predators or move between tide pools.

children.description: Palaemonid shrimps are a diverse family of small to medium-sized shrimps found in both freshwater and marine environments. They are characterized by their slender bodies, long antennae, and distinctive rostrum (pointed projection) extending from their head. Most species are excellent swimmers and play important roles as both predators of small organisms and prey for larger fish.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other shrimp families, palaemonids typically have a prominent, toothed rostrum and their second pair of walking legs (pereiopods) are often longer and more robust than the first pair.
children.funFact: Many palaemonid shrimps, including the Glass Shrimps found in New England, are nearly transparent, making them incredibly difficult to spot in the water despite being relatively common.

children.name: Paguridae
Pagurus
children.description: Pagurus hermit crabs are the classic shell-dwelling crabs you're most likely to encounter along New England shores. These fascinating crustaceans protect their soft, vulnerable abdomens by carrying around empty snail shells, switching to larger shells as they grow. They're active scavengers and predators, using their claws to tear apart food and defend their portable homes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other hermit crab groups, Pagurus species have their left claw typically larger than their right claw, and their eyestalks are usually longer than wide. Their antennae and walking legs also show distinctive proportions that help distinguish them from other hermit crab genera.
children.funFact: When a Pagurus hermit crab finds a shell that's too big for them, they'll often wait by it for hours or even days until a larger crab shows up, creating a "vacancy chain" where multiple crabs trade up to better-fitting shells in sequence!

children.description: Pagurid hermit crabs are the most common and familiar hermit crabs found along New England's coast. These fascinating crustaceans have soft, curved abdomens that they protect by living inside empty snail shells, which they carry around like portable homes. As they grow, they must find larger shells to move into, often engaging in complex shell-swapping chains with other hermit crabs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other hermit crab families, pagurids have left-handed (asymmetrical) claws with the left claw typically being larger than the right. They also have well-developed walking legs and can completely withdraw into their adopted shells when threatened.
children.funFact: When a hermit crab finds a shell that's too big for it but perfect for a larger crab, it will wait by the shell and attract other crabs to form a 'vacancy chain' where each crab moves into the next-largest shell in sequence, like a housing market for crustaceans!

children.name: Panopeidae
Dyspanopeus
children.description: Dyspanopeus is a genus of small mud crabs that live in shallow coastal waters and estuaries. These compact crabs are well-adapted to muddy environments where they burrow and scavenge for food along the seafloor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their relatively small size and robust, somewhat flattened shell that helps them navigate through soft sediments.
children.funFact: Despite their small size, these mud crabs are important ecosystem engineers that help aerate sediments through their burrowing activities.

children.name: Panopeus
children.description: Mud crabs are small, hardy crabs that live in muddy coastal areas like salt marshes, oyster beds, and tidal flats. They are excellent burrowers and can tolerate varying water conditions, from brackish to fully saltwater environments. These compact crabs are well-adapted to life in soft sediments where they hunt for small prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mud crabs have distinctively thick, robust claws and a somewhat flattened, oval-shaped shell that helps them navigate through mud and sediment. Their dark coloration provides excellent camouflage against muddy substrates.
children.funFact: Despite their small size, mud crabs are surprisingly strong and can deliver a painful pinch - they're sometimes called 'stone crabs' by locals because of their rock-hard grip!

children.name: Rhithropanopeus
children.description: Rhithropanopeus is a genus of small mud crabs that live in estuaries and brackish water environments. These crabs are typically found burrowing in muddy sediments along shorelines and in salt marshes, where they feed on algae, small invertebrates, and organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their relatively small size, brownish coloration that helps them blend with muddy substrates, and their ability to tolerate varying salinity levels in estuarine environments.
children.funFact: The White-tipped Mud Crab is actually an invasive species that was accidentally introduced to New England waters from the Gulf of Mexico and has successfully established populations throughout the region's estuaries.

children.name: Eurypanopeus
children.description: Eurypanopeus is a genus of small, flattened mud crabs that live in shallow coastal waters and estuaries. These hardy crabs are well-adapted to life in muddy, low-oxygen environments where they burrow and forage for food.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their notably flattened, oval-shaped shells and relatively small size compared to other mud crabs. Their compressed body shape helps them navigate through tight spaces in muddy sediments.
children.funFact: The Flatback Mud Crab can survive in waters with very low oxygen levels by using specialized gills that can extract oxygen more efficiently than most other crab species.

children.name: Hexapanopeus
children.description: Hexapanopeus is a genus of small, sturdy mud crabs that live in estuarine and coastal marine environments. These crabs are well-adapted to life in muddy sediments and shallow waters where they burrow and feed on organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their relatively smooth, rectangular carapace and robust claws that are well-suited for digging in soft substrates.
children.funFact: The Smooth Mud Crab can survive in waters with varying salinity levels, making it perfectly suited for life in New England's tidal marshes and estuaries where fresh and salt water mix.

children.description: Mud crabs are small, sturdy crabs that live in shallow coastal waters, muddy shores, and estuaries throughout New England. They have thick, powerful claws and robust shells that help them survive in harsh intertidal environments where they burrow in mud and hide under rocks.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other crab families, mud crabs have distinctively heavy, unequal-sized claws and thick, somewhat flattened shells. Their carapace is typically wider than it is long, giving them a characteristically broad appearance.
children.funFact: Some mud crabs can tolerate dramatic changes in salinity, allowing them to thrive in brackish estuaries where freshwater rivers meet the sea - conditions that would stress or kill many other marine creatures.

children.name: Pinnotheridae
Pinnixa
children.description: Pinnixa is a genus of small pea crabs that live as symbionts inside the tubes or burrows of marine worms, mollusks, and other invertebrates. These tiny crabs have soft, often translucent shells and are specially adapted for their commensal lifestyle, depending on their hosts for shelter and food scraps.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pinnixa crabs are distinguished by their small size, soft carapace, and highly specialized lifestyle living within host organisms. Unlike free-living crabs, they have reduced defensive structures and rely entirely on their hosts for protection.
children.funFact: Female Pinnixa crabs are often much larger than males and may spend their entire adult lives inside a single host's burrow, with the tiny males visiting only to mate.

children.name: Tumidotheres
children.description: Tumidotheres is a genus of small crabs that have evolved to live as commensals inside the shells of bivalve mollusks like oysters and mussels. These tiny crabs have soft, rounded bodies that allow them to squeeze into their host's shell where they feed on food particles filtered by their host. They represent a fascinating example of how some crabs have adapted to live symbiotically with other marine animals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike free-living crabs, Tumidotheres species have notably soft, flexible shells and compact, rounded body shapes that allow them to fit inside bivalve shells. Their reduced shell hardness and specialized body proportions clearly separate them from typical hard-shelled shore crabs.
children.funFact: The female Squatter Pea Crab can grow much larger than the male and may become permanently trapped inside her host's shell as she matures, relying on tiny males to find her for reproduction.

children.name: Tubicolixa
children.description: Tubicolixa is a genus of tiny pea crabs that have evolved a specialized lifestyle living inside the tubes of marine worms. These small crabs are commensal organisms, meaning they benefit from their worm hosts without causing harm by feeding on food particles that flow through the worm's tube.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other pea crabs that typically live inside bivalve shells, Tubicolixa species are uniquely adapted to life within the protective tubes of polychaete worms. Their bodies are specially modified to fit within these narrow, cylindrical spaces.
children.funFact: The tube pea crab is so small and well-adapted to its tubular home that it can live its entire adult life within a single worm tube, essentially turning the tube into its own personal dining room where it intercepts food meant for its host.

children.name: Pinnotheres
children.description: Pinnotheres is a genus of tiny crabs known as pea crabs that live as symbionts inside the shells of mollusks like oysters, mussels, and clams. These small, soft-bodied crabs have evolved to spend their entire adult lives within their host's shell, feeding on plankton and organic matter that the host filters from the water. They represent one of nature's most intimate partnerships between crustaceans and mollusks.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pea crabs in this genus have unusually soft, thin shells compared to other crabs, which allows them to move easily within their host's confined space. Their small size (typically less than half an inch) and pale coloration help them remain inconspicuous within their mollusk homes.
children.funFact: Female pea crabs can grow much larger than males and may spend their entire adult lives inside a single oyster or clam, while the tiny males must venture out to find mates.

children.name: Zaops
children.description: Zaops is a genus of tiny parasitic crabs that live inside the shells of mollusks like oysters and mussels. These small, soft-bodied crabs have evolved to spend their entire adult lives as commensals or parasites within their host's shell cavity. They feed on food particles filtered by their host and have become highly specialized for this unique lifestyle.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike free-living crabs, Zaops have soft, rounded bodies with reduced shells that allow them to fit comfortably inside mollusk shells. Their legs are adapted for clinging to the soft tissues of their hosts rather than for walking or swimming.
children.funFact: Female oyster pea crabs can grow much larger than males because they need to carry eggs, while the tiny males often remain permanently attached to the female's body.

children.description: Bivalve pea crabs are tiny crabs that have evolved a unique lifestyle of living inside the shells of bivalves like clams, mussels, and oysters. These small, soft-bodied crabs spend most or all of their lives as commensals, benefiting from the protection and food particles filtered by their host without necessarily harming them. They represent one of nature's most specialized examples of symbiotic living.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other crabs, pea crabs have extremely soft, thin shells and are typically very small (often pea-sized, hence their name). Their bodies are adapted for life in confined spaces, with females often being much larger and more sedentary than males.
children.funFact: Female pea crabs can become so large and soft that they may become permanently trapped inside their host's shell, spending their entire adult lives in this cozy but confining home!

children.name: Ocypodidae
Minuca
children.description: Minuca is a genus of fiddler crabs found in coastal salt marshes and mudflats throughout New England. These small crabs are famous for the males' dramatically oversized claw, which they wave in the air to attract mates and defend their territory. They live in burrows they dig in the muddy or sandy substrate near the water's edge.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Minuca fiddler crabs are distinguished from other fiddler crab genera by their specific claw shapes, carapace patterns, and habitat preferences. They tend to prefer muddier substrates compared to some other fiddler crab groups that favor sandier areas.
children.funFact: A male fiddler crab's giant claw can weigh up to half of his total body weight, making it quite the burden to carry around just to impress the ladies!

children.name: Leptuca
children.description: Leptuca is a genus of small fiddler crabs that live in salt marshes and sandy shores along the Atlantic coast. These crabs are known for the dramatic size difference between their claws - males have one enormously enlarged claw that they wave to attract mates and defend territory. They are semi-terrestrial, spending time both in burrows they dig in the sand and foraging on the surface at low tide.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Leptuca crabs can be distinguished from other fiddler crab genera by their relatively narrow carapace (shell) and the specific shape and proportions of their enlarged claw in males. They also tend to prefer sandier habitats compared to some other fiddler crab groups that favor muddier environments.
children.funFact: Male Leptuca crabs can regenerate their giant claw if they lose it, but the replacement claw will grow on the opposite side of their body from where the original was located.

children.name: Ocypode
children.description: Ghost crabs are fast-moving crabs that live in burrows on sandy beaches and can survive both in water and on land. They get their name from their pale, sand-colored shells that help them blend in with beach environments, making them appear almost ghostly as they scurry across the sand.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most crabs, ghost crabs have eyes on tall stalks that can be folded down into grooves, and they can run sideways at speeds up to 10 mph on their long, powerful legs.
children.funFact: Ghost crabs can hold their breath for up to 6 weeks by storing water in special gill chambers, allowing them to live far from the ocean while still breathing through gills like fish.

children.description: Ghost and fiddler crabs are semi-terrestrial crabs that spend much of their time on land, though they still need to return to water to reproduce. These active crabs are excellent diggers, creating elaborate burrows in sandy beaches, mudflats, and salt marshes where they retreat during high tide and cold weather.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most crabs, members of this family have adapted to life primarily on land and can run remarkably fast across sand and mud. Many species have specialized gills that can extract oxygen from both water and moist air.
children.funFact: Male fiddler crabs have one dramatically oversized claw that can weigh up to half their body weight, which they wave like a semaphore flag to attract mates and warn off rivals.

children.name: Thoridae
Eualus
children.description: Eualus is a genus of small, delicate shrimp that live in the cold waters of the North Atlantic and Arctic oceans. These tiny crustaceans are typically found scuttling along the seafloor or swimming in shallow coastal waters, where they feed on small particles and organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Eualus shrimp are distinguished by their small size, translucent bodies, and characteristic curved rostrum (pointed snout-like projection). They have a more delicate build compared to many other marine shrimp species.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, Eualus shrimp play an important role in marine food webs, serving as food for fish, seabirds, and other marine creatures while helping to recycle nutrients on the ocean floor.

children.name: Lebbeus
children.description: Lebbeus is a genus of small, deep-water shrimp that live in cold marine environments. These shrimp are characterized by their spiny appearance and are typically found crawling along the ocean floor in northern waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Lebbeus are distinguished by their prominent spines along the body and rostrum (pointed snout), which give them a more armored appearance compared to smoother shrimp species.
children.funFact: The Spiny Lebbeid shrimp can survive in the frigid waters of the North Atlantic by producing antifreeze proteins that prevent ice crystals from forming in their body fluids.

children.description: Thoridae is a family of small, delicate shrimp that live in cold ocean waters. These tiny crustaceans are typically found in deeper waters along the New England coast, where they scuttle along the seafloor or swim in small groups near the bottom.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Thoridae shrimp are distinguished from other shrimp families by their small size, slender build, and distinctive rostrum (pointed projection from the head). They also have a characteristic hump-backed appearance and relatively long, thin legs.
children.funFact: Some Thoridae shrimp can change color to match their surroundings, shifting from translucent to reddish or brownish hues depending on the substrate they're living on.

children.name: Pandalidae
Pandalus
children.description: Pandalus is a genus of cold-water shrimp found in northern seas, including the waters off New England. These are commercially important marine crustaceans that live on or near the ocean floor, typically in deeper waters where temperatures remain consistently cool.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pandalus shrimp have a distinctive curved body shape and long, slender antennae. They can be distinguished from other shrimp genera by their specific arrangement of spines on their carapace (shell) and their particular swimming and feeding behaviors.
children.funFact: Many Pandalus shrimp are sequential hermaphrodites, starting life as males and later transforming into females as they grow larger and older.

children.name: Dichelopandalus
children.description: Dichelopandalus is a genus of small marine shrimp-like crustaceans that live in the cold waters of the North Atlantic. These tiny creatures are part of the mysid shrimp family and are important members of the ocean's zooplankton community, serving as food for fish and other marine animals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their elongated, beak-like rostrum (front projection) and distinctive bristle-like structures on their bodies. They can be distinguished from other mysid shrimp by their specific body proportions and the arrangement of spines on their tail segments.
children.funFact: Despite being only about 15-20 millimeters long, Dichelopandalus shrimp are excellent swimmers that can quickly dart through the water column using synchronized movements of their swimming legs called pleopods.

children.description: Pandalid shrimp are marine crustaceans that live in cold ocean waters, particularly in the North Atlantic and North Pacific. These shrimp are commercially important and include species commonly known as northern shrimp or pink shrimp. They are bottom-dwelling creatures that feed on small organisms and organic matter on the seafloor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pandalid shrimp have a distinctive rostrum (pointed projection) extending from their head and possess a characteristic body shape with a curved abdomen. They can be distinguished from other shrimp families by their specific gill structure and the arrangement of their walking legs.
children.funFact: Many pandalid shrimp are sequential hermaphrodites, meaning they start life as males and later change into females as they grow larger and older.

children.name: Varunidae
Hemigrapsus
children.description: Hemigrapsus is a genus of small to medium-sized shore crabs that are well-adapted to life in rocky intertidal zones and shallow coastal waters. These crabs are characterized by their square-shaped shells and ability to tolerate varying salinity levels, making them successful in estuarine environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Hemigrapsus can be distinguished from other shore crabs by their relatively flat, square carapace and the presence of distinctive brush-like hairs on their claws and legs.
children.funFact: The Asian Shore Crab arrived in New England waters as a stowaway in ship ballast water in the 1980s and has since become one of the most abundant crab species along our rocky shores.

children.name: Eriocheir
children.description: Eriocheir is a genus of freshwater crabs commonly known as mitten crabs due to the dense, furry patches of hair on their claws that resemble mittens. These medium-sized crabs are native to East Asia but have become invasive species in many parts of the world, including New England waterways. They spend most of their adult lives in freshwater rivers and lakes but must return to saltwater to reproduce.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The distinctive dense patches of hair or setae covering their claws easily distinguish mitten crabs from other freshwater crabs. They also have a relatively square-shaped carapace and strong, well-developed claws compared to many other freshwater crab species.
children.funFact: Chinese mitten crabs can travel hundreds of miles between freshwater and saltwater environments, and they're surprisingly good climbers - they can even scale vertical surfaces like dam walls using their strong claws!

children.description: Varunid crabs are a family of small to medium-sized crabs that are well-adapted to life in coastal environments. These hardy crabs can be found in various habitats including rocky shores, mudflats, and marshes, where they scurry about searching for food like algae, small invertebrates, and organic debris.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Varunid crabs typically have a somewhat square-shaped shell (carapace) and relatively thick, sturdy legs that help them navigate rocky surfaces and burrow in sediment. Their eye stalks are usually short and their claws are often unequal in size.
children.funFact: Some varunid crabs, like the Chinese mitten crab, are famous travelers that can migrate hundreds of miles between freshwater breeding areas and saltwater coastal habitats during their lifetime.

children.name: Cancridae
Cancer
children.description: Cancer is a genus of robust, commercially important crabs known for their thick, oval-shaped shells and powerful claws. These hardy crabs are found in rocky and sandy coastal waters, where they scavenge for food and prey on shellfish, worms, and other small marine creatures. Both New England species are prized as seafood and play important ecological roles as both predators and scavengers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cancer crabs are distinguished by their broad, smooth carapace with distinctively serrated (saw-toothed) edges along the front margin. Their heavy, unequal claws and relatively short walking legs give them a stocky, powerful appearance compared to other crab genera.
children.funFact: The genus name 'Cancer' means 'crab' in Latin and is the same word used for the zodiac constellation - ancient astronomers thought the star pattern looked like a crab!

children.description: Rock crabs are robust, hard-shelled crabs that live primarily in rocky coastal areas and deeper waters. They are characterized by their oval-shaped carapaces (shells) and powerful claws that they use for crushing shellfish and other prey. These crabs are typically larger and more heavily built than many other crab families.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Rock crabs can be distinguished from other crab families by their broad, oval carapaces with smooth or slightly granulated surfaces and their notably heavy, unequal claws. Unlike some other crabs, they lack prominent spines on their shells and have a more streamlined appearance.
children.funFact: The Jonah crab, one of New England's rock crabs, can live for over 20 years and has become increasingly valuable to fishermen as lobster populations have declined in some areas.

children.name: Geryonidae
Ovalipes
children.description: Ovalipes is a genus of swimming crabs known for their distinctive oval-shaped shells and powerful swimming abilities. These crabs are well-adapted for life in sandy coastal waters, where they can quickly bury themselves in sediment when threatened.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other crabs, Ovalipes have flattened, paddle-like rear legs that make them excellent swimmers rather than just bottom-walkers.
children.funFact: The Ocellate Lady Crab gets its name from the eye-like spots (ocelli) on its shell, which may help confuse predators about which direction the crab is facing.

children.name: Chaceon
children.description: Chaceon is a genus of deep-sea crabs that live in the cold, dark waters of the continental shelf and slope. These robust crabs are specially adapted for life in the deep ocean, where they scavenge for food on the seafloor. They are commercially important as they are harvested for their meat in many parts of the world.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Chaceon crabs have a broad, oval-shaped carapace and strong, powerful claws that help them navigate and feed in the deep-sea environment. Unlike shallow-water crabs, they have adaptations for the high-pressure, low-temperature conditions of the deep ocean.
children.funFact: Red deepsea crabs can live for over 40 years and don't reach sexual maturity until they're around 7-9 years old, making them one of the longest-lived crab species in New England waters.

children.description: Geryonidae is a family of deep-water crabs that live primarily in the ocean's depths, from the continental shelf down to abyssal plains. These crabs are characterized by their flattened, oval-shaped bodies and long, slender legs that help them navigate the seafloor. Most species in this family are commercially important and are harvested for food in various parts of the world.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Geryonid crabs can be distinguished from other crab families by their distinctly flattened carapace (shell) that is wider than it is long, and their unusually long walking legs relative to their body size. Their eyes are also positioned on short, thick eyestalks.
children.funFact: The lady crab (Ovalipes ocellatus) can actually swim by rapidly paddling its flattened hind legs, making it one of the few truly swimming crabs in New England waters.

children.name: Epialtidae
Libinia
children.description: Libinia is a genus of spider crabs found along the Atlantic coast, including New England waters. These crabs are known for their triangular shells and long, spindly legs that give them a spider-like appearance. They are bottom-dwelling crabs that often camouflage themselves with algae, sponges, and other marine debris.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Libinia spider crabs have distinctively pointed, triangular carapaces (shells) and exceptionally long, thin legs relative to their body size. Their shells also feature prominent spines and ridges that help distinguish them from other crab families.
children.funFact: These clever crabs are master decorators, actively attaching seaweed, barnacles, and other marine organisms to their shells using special hooked hairs, creating living camouflage that helps them blend seamlessly into their surroundings.

children.description: Kelp crabs are spider-like marine crabs with long, thin legs and triangular or pear-shaped bodies. They are well-adapted for living among seaweeds and other marine vegetation, where their slender build helps them navigate through tight spaces. These crabs are often found clinging to kelp, eelgrass, and other underwater plants in coastal waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical shore crabs with broad, flat bodies, kelp crabs have distinctively long, spindly legs that can span several times their body width. Their triangular carapace (shell) is much narrower than most other crab families.
children.funFact: Kelp crabs are master decorators - they camouflage themselves by attaching bits of seaweed, sponges, and other marine debris to hook-like hairs on their shells, making them nearly invisible among the plants they call home.

children.name: Oregoniidae
Hyas
children.description: Lyre crabs are a group of spider crabs known for their distinctive triangular, lyre-shaped carapace (shell) and long, spindly legs. These cold-water crabs are found in the deeper waters of the North Atlantic, where they scavenge along the seafloor for food. Both New England species are excellent at camouflaging themselves by decorating their shells with algae, sponges, and other marine debris.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lyre crabs can be identified by their uniquely shaped carapace that resembles a musical lyre, with a narrow front end that widens toward the back. Their legs are proportionally longer and more slender than most other crab species in New England waters.
children.funFact: Lyre crabs are master decorators - they carefully select and attach pieces of seaweed, hydroids, and sponges to their shells using special hooked hairs, creating living camouflage that grows and changes along with their environment.

children.description: Oregoniidae is a family of spider crabs found in cold northern waters, including the North Atlantic and North Pacific. These crabs are characterized by their triangular, pointed carapaces (shells) and long, slender legs that give them a spider-like appearance. They are typically found in deeper, cooler waters where they scavenge for food on the ocean floor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family have distinctively triangular shells that come to a sharp point at the front, along with exceptionally long, thin legs relative to their body size. Their shells are often covered with spines, bumps, or tubercles that help distinguish them from other crab families.
children.funFact: Lyre crabs in this family are sometimes called 'decorator crabs' because they camouflage themselves by attaching seaweed, sponges, and other marine debris to their shells using hooked hairs.

children.name: Hippolytidae
Hippolyte
children.description: Hippolyte is a genus of small, translucent shrimp that are masters of camouflage in marine environments. These delicate crustaceans have slender bodies and long, thin legs that help them navigate through underwater vegetation. They are part of the larger family of grass shrimp and are typically found in shallow coastal waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Hippolyte can be distinguished from other grass shrimp by their extremely transparent bodies and their ability to change color to match their surroundings. They also have characteristically long, thread-like antennae that can be longer than their entire body.
children.funFact: Hippolyte shrimp can change their color and pattern within minutes to perfectly match the seagrass, algae, or other marine plants they're hiding among, making them nearly invisible to both predators and prey.

children.name: Latreutes
children.description: Latreutes is a genus of small marine shrimp that are specially adapted for life among floating seaweed. These tiny crustaceans have evolved unique features that help them blend in perfectly with their sargassum seaweed homes in the open ocean.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most shrimp that live on the seafloor, Latreutes species have flattened bodies and leaf-like appendages that perfectly mimic the appearance of seaweed fronds, making them nearly invisible among their floating habitat.
children.funFact: Sargassum shrimp are so well-camouflaged that they can change their color and body posture to match different parts of the seaweed, from brown stems to yellowish air bladders.

children.description: Hump-backed shrimps are small marine crustaceans named for the distinctive curved or humped shape of their back (carapace). These delicate shrimps are typically found among seaweeds, sea grasses, and other marine vegetation where they blend in perfectly with their surroundings. They are active swimmers that feed on small organic particles and algae.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The characteristic hump or curve in their back section sets them apart from other shrimp families. They also have a compressed body shape and long, slender antennae that help them navigate through dense vegetation.
children.funFact: Many hump-backed shrimps are masters of camouflage, able to change their color and pattern to match the seaweed or algae they live on, making them nearly invisible to both predators and prey.

children.name: Penaeidae
Penaeus
children.description: Penaeus is a genus of large, commercially important shrimp found in warm coastal waters. These shrimp are characterized by their robust bodies, long antennae, and distinctive grooved shells that give them their common name of 'grooved shrimp.'
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other shrimp genera, Penaeus species have a distinctive groove running along the back of their shell and lack teeth on the lower edge of their rostrum (the pointed projection from their head).
children.funFact: Northern brown shrimp can grow up to 9 inches long and are capable of jumping backwards at speeds up to 25 body lengths per second when escaping predators!

children.description: Penaeid prawns are marine shrimp that live in coastal waters and are among the most economically important shellfish in the world. These crustaceans have elongated bodies, long antennae, and powerful swimming tails that help them navigate ocean currents. Most species prefer warm, shallow waters near coastlines where they feed on small organisms and organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other shrimp families, penaeid prawns release their eggs directly into the water column rather than carrying them attached to their bodies. They also have a distinctive rostrum (pointed projection) that extends forward from their head.
children.funFact: Penaeid prawns undergo dramatic migrations, with some species traveling hundreds of miles from shallow nursery areas to deeper offshore waters as they mature.

children.name: Carcinidae
Carcinus
children.description: Green crabs are medium-sized shore crabs known for their distinctive greenish coloration and aggressive nature. They are hardy crabs that can tolerate a wide range of water conditions, from fully marine to brackish environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Green crabs can be identified by their five sharp spines along each side of their shell and their characteristic mottled green color, though they can also appear orange or red.
children.funFact: European Green Crabs are one of the world's most successful marine invaders, having spread from their native Atlantic European waters to coastlines on every continent except Antarctica.

children.description: Carcinidae is a family of shore crabs that are well-adapted to life in coastal waters and intertidal zones. These crabs are characterized by their broad, flattened shells and strong claws that help them navigate rocky shores and sandy bottoms. They are typically aggressive predators and scavengers that play important ecological roles in marine ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family have distinctively broad, somewhat hexagonal carapaces (shells) with prominent teeth along the front edge. Their last pair of walking legs are flattened and paddle-like, making them excellent swimmers compared to many other crab families.
children.funFact: The European Green Crab in this family is considered one of the world's most successful marine invaders, having established populations on every continent except Antarctica!

children.name: Nephropidae
Homarus
children.description: Homarus is a genus of large marine lobsters that are among the most recognizable crustaceans in New England waters. These lobsters are characterized by their robust bodies, large claws, and ability to grow to impressive sizes over their long lifespans.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Homarus have two distinctly different claws - one larger 'crusher' claw for breaking shells and one smaller 'cutter' claw with sharp edges for tearing food. They also lack the fan-shaped tail found in spiny lobsters and have long antennae.
children.funFact: American lobsters can live over 100 years and continue growing throughout their lives, with the largest recorded specimen weighing over 44 pounds!

children.description: True lobsters are large marine crustaceans with robust bodies, long antennae, and powerful claws. They live on the ocean floor, typically in rocky crevices or burrows, and are skilled scavengers and predators that feed on fish, mollusks, and other crustaceans.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other lobster-like creatures, true lobsters have asymmetrical claws - one larger crusher claw and one smaller cutting claw - and lack the flattened tail fan found in spiny lobsters.
children.funFact: American lobsters can live over 100 years and continue growing throughout their lives by molting their hard shell, with some specimens reaching weights of over 40 pounds.

children.name: Hippidae
Emerita
children.description: Sand fleas are small, egg-shaped crustaceans that live in the sandy surf zone of ocean beaches. These fascinating creatures are perfectly adapted for life in the constantly shifting sand where waves crash, using their specialized legs to quickly burrow backwards into the sand as waves recede.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other crabs, sand fleas have a smooth, dome-shaped shell and lack large claws, instead having feathery antennae that they use to filter food particles from the water.
children.funFact: Sand fleas can burrow completely into wet sand in just 1.5 seconds, making them appear to vanish instantly as waves wash over them.

children.description: Hippid mole crabs are small, egg-shaped crustaceans that live buried in sandy beaches along the surf zone. They have specialized adaptations for life in the sand, including flattened bodies and powerful digging appendages that allow them to quickly burrow backwards into the sand as waves wash over them.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical crabs with hard shells and prominent claws, mole crabs have soft, rounded bodies with reduced or absent claws and short antennae adapted for filter feeding in turbulent surf.
children.funFact: These remarkable crustaceans can dig backwards into wet sand in just seconds, disappearing completely as each wave recedes, then emerging to filter-feed as the next wave approaches.

children.name: Crangonidae
Crangon
children.description: Crangon is a genus of small, translucent shrimp that are perfectly adapted for life on sandy ocean bottoms. These marine crustaceans are masters of camouflage, able to quickly bury themselves in sand and change color to match their surroundings. They're active predators and scavengers, feeding on small worms, crustaceans, and organic debris on the seafloor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other shrimp, Crangon species have a flattened body shape and specialized front claws (chelae) that are perfectly designed for digging and capturing prey in sandy environments. Their eyes are positioned on top of their head, allowing them to watch for predators and prey while mostly buried in sand.
children.funFact: Sand shrimp can change color from nearly transparent to brown or gray in just a few minutes to perfectly match the sand they're hiding in, making them almost invisible to both predators and prey.

children.description: Crangonidae are a family of small, sand-dwelling shrimp commonly known as sand shrimp or brown shrimp. These marine crustaceans are masters of camouflage, burying themselves in sandy or muddy bottoms of shallow coastal waters where they blend in perfectly with their surroundings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sand shrimp have a distinctively flattened body shape and can rapidly change color to match the sediment they're hiding in. Unlike many other shrimp families, they have asymmetrical claws with one larger claw used for digging and capturing prey.
children.funFact: Sand shrimp can bury themselves completely in sand in just seconds, leaving only their eyes and antennae exposed to watch for both prey and predators!

children.name: Sesarmidae
Sesarma
children.description: American Marsh Crabs are small, semi-terrestrial crabs that live in salt marshes and coastal wetlands. These hardy crabs are excellent climbers and can survive both in water and on land, spending much of their time burrowing in muddy marsh banks and feeding on marsh grasses and decomposing plant matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most marine crabs, Sesarma crabs have adapted to life in the intertidal zone with the ability to breathe air for extended periods and climb vertical surfaces like marsh grass stems and wooden pilings.
children.funFact: Purple Marsh Crabs are considered ecosystem engineers because their burrowing activity helps aerate marsh sediments and their grazing on marsh grasses can significantly influence the structure of salt marsh plant communities.

children.description: Sesarmid marsh crabs are semi-terrestrial crabs that live in coastal salt marshes, mangroves, and other brackish water environments. These hardy crabs can survive both in water and on land, spending much of their time burrowing in muddy banks and feeding on plant matter and detritus. They play important roles as both scavengers and prey in their marsh ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most marine crabs, sesarmids have adapted to life in low-salinity environments and can breathe air for extended periods. Their square-shaped carapace and strong claws help distinguish them from other crab families.
children.funFact: These crabs are excellent climbers and can often be seen scaling vertical surfaces like dock pilings, rocks, and even mangrove roots with surprising agility.

children.name: Upogebiidae
Upogebia
children.description: Mudprawns are small, lobster-like crustaceans that spend their lives burrowing in soft mud and sand of coastal areas. These industrious creatures create extensive tunnel systems in the seafloor, where they filter-feed on organic particles and small organisms from the surrounding sediment.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true lobsters, mudprawns have much more delicate claws and softer bodies adapted for their burrowing lifestyle. Their flattened bodies and specialized digging appendages make them perfectly suited for life underground in marine sediments.
children.funFact: A single mudprawn can move up to 24 liters of sediment per day while maintaining its burrow system, making them important ecosystem engineers that help oxygenate the seafloor.

children.description: Upogebiidae is a family of small, shrimp-like crustaceans commonly known as mudprawns or mud lobsters. These marine creatures are specialized burrowers that spend most of their lives in U-shaped tunnels they dig in soft sediments like mud and sand on ocean floors. They have elongated bodies with powerful claws that help them excavate their underground homes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mudprawns can be distinguished from other burrowing crustaceans by their unequal claws (one is typically larger than the other) and their flattened, spade-like tail fans that help them move sediment while digging.
children.funFact: A single mudprawn can move up to 24 liters of sediment per day while maintaining its burrow, making them important ecosystem engineers that help aerate seafloor sediments.

children.name: Porcellanidae
Polyonyx
children.description: Polyonyx is a genus of small porcelain crabs that are commensal, meaning they live peacefully alongside other marine animals for mutual benefit. These tiny crabs are typically found living within the tubes or burrows of marine worms, where they filter-feed on plankton and organic particles from the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Polyonyx crabs have flattened, rounded bodies and characteristically long, feathery antennae that they use for filter-feeding. Unlike many other crabs, they have a more crab-like appearance compared to their porcelain crab relatives, with a less elongated body shape.
children.funFact: Despite being called porcelain crabs, Polyonyx and their relatives are more closely related to lobsters than true crabs, and they can detach their claws when threatened, leaving predators with just a claw while they escape to safety.

children.description: Porcelain crabs are small, flattened crustaceans that aren't actually true crabs despite their name. They have a distinctive crab-like appearance with a broad, smooth carapace (shell) and long antennae that they use to filter feed on plankton and organic particles from the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true crabs, porcelain crabs have a visible tail (abdomen) that's folded under their body and can be easily seen, plus they have only three pairs of walking legs instead of four.
children.funFact: When threatened, porcelain crabs can quickly drop their claws and scuttle backward to escape predators, later regenerating the lost appendages.

children.name: Calappidae
Calappa
children.description: Typical Box Crabs are fascinating crustaceans with distinctively flattened, box-like shells that give them their common name. These crabs are masters of camouflage, often burying themselves in sand or mud with only their eyes and antennae visible above the surface. They have specially adapted claws that can fold tightly against their body, creating a smooth, streamlined shape.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Box crabs are easily recognized by their extremely flattened, almost rectangular carapace and their ability to completely retract their legs and claws underneath their shell. Unlike most crabs, their shell edges are thin and sharp, almost like the lid of a box.
children.funFact: When threatened, box crabs can fold their legs and claws so tightly under their shell that they become nearly impossible for predators to grab, essentially turning themselves into a living armored box.

children.description: Box crabs are distinctive marine crabs known for their unique defensive behavior and specialized shell shape. When threatened, they can tuck their claws and legs tightly against their body, creating a smooth, box-like appearance that protects their soft parts. These crabs are typically found in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms where they burrow and feed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Box crabs have a broad, flattened carapace (shell) with wing-like extensions that help them dig into sediment. Their claws can fold perfectly against their body to create a seamless defensive posture, unlike most other crab families.
children.funFact: When a box crab feels threatened, it can completely seal itself up like a living puzzle box, with its claws fitting so perfectly against its body that predators can't find any gaps to attack!

children.name: Lysmatidae
Lysmata
children.description: Lysmata is a genus of small, colorful marine shrimp known as cleaner shrimp. These tropical and subtropical species are famous for their symbiotic relationships with fish, providing cleaning services by removing parasites and dead skin from their clients.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other shrimp, Lysmata species are hermaphrodites that can change sex, and they have distinctive long, white antennae along with bright striped or spotted coloration patterns.
children.funFact: Lysmata shrimp are sequential hermaphrodites - they start life as males but can transform into females when needed for reproduction, and some can even switch back and forth between sexes!

children.description: Lysmatidae is a family of small, colorful marine shrimp known for their cleaning behavior and unique reproductive strategies. These shrimp are commonly found in tropical and subtropical waters, where they often live among coral reefs and rocky crevices. They are popular in the aquarium trade due to their striking appearance and beneficial cleaning services.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their elongated rostrum (pointed snout), distinctive color patterns with stripes or spots, and specialized cleaning appendages. Unlike many other shrimp families, lysmatids are sequential hermaphrodites, meaning they can change sex during their lifetime.
children.funFact: Many Lysmatidae species operate 'cleaning stations' on coral reefs, where fish line up to have parasites and dead tissue removed by the shrimp's delicate claws and mouthparts.

children.name: Parthenopidae
Heterocrypta
children.description: Heterocrypta is a genus of small crabs that are known for their ability to camouflage themselves by decorating their shells with bits of sponge, algae, and other marine debris. These decorator crabs are part of the spider crab family and are found in shallow coastal waters. They use their specialized hooked setae (bristles) to attach materials to their carapace, creating an effective disguise.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Heterocrypta crabs are distinguished by their triangular carapace and their exceptional ability to camouflage using attached organic materials. Unlike many other crabs, they actively collect and arrange decorative materials on their shells rather than relying solely on natural coloration.
children.funFact: Heterocrypta crabs are such dedicated decorators that they will carefully transfer their camouflage materials from their old shell to their new one each time they molt, essentially redecorating their entire home!

children.description: Elbow crabs are a distinctive family of marine crabs known for their uniquely shaped claws and legs that bend at sharp angles, giving them their common name. These crabs have triangular or spider-like body shapes and often have decorative spines or bumps covering their shells. They are typically small to medium-sized crabs that live on the ocean floor in coastal waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Elbow crabs can be identified by their characteristically bent, angular legs and claws that stick out at odd angles from their bodies. Their carapace (shell) is often triangular and wider than it is long, unlike the more rounded shells of many other crab families.
children.funFact: Many elbow crabs are master decorators, attaching pieces of sponge, algae, and other marine organisms to their shells as camouflage to blend in with their surroundings on the seafloor.

children.name: Grapsidae
Planes
children.description: Planes is a genus of small marine crabs that have adapted to live on floating objects in the open ocean. These crabs are specialized for life at sea, clinging to seaweed, driftwood, and other floating debris as they drift with ocean currents.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical shore crabs, Planes crabs have flattened bodies and strong claws perfectly adapted for gripping smooth, floating surfaces in rough ocean waters.
children.funFact: Gulfweed crabs are sometimes called "Columbus crabs" because sailors reported seeing them clinging to floating sargassum seaweed during early Atlantic crossings.

children.description: Shore crabs are a family of crabs that live in coastal marine environments, typically found in shallow waters near shorelines. These crabs are well-adapted to life between the tides and in nearshore habitats, where they can handle changes in salinity and water levels.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Shore crabs have a relatively square-shaped carapace (shell) and strong, sturdy legs that help them navigate rocky shores and sandy bottoms. Their eyes are positioned on short stalks, and they typically have a more flattened body compared to many other crab families.
children.funFact: The single New England species in this family, Planes minutus, is known as the Columbus crab because it's often found floating on sargassum seaweed in the open ocean, essentially hitchhiking across vast distances just like early ocean explorers.

children.name: Callianassidae
Gilvossius
children.description: Gilvossius is a genus of small, burrowing crustaceans known as mud shrimp that live in soft sediments along coastlines. These industrious creatures spend their lives digging extensive tunnel systems in muddy or sandy bottoms of shallow marine waters. They are filter feeders that help process organic matter in coastal ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Gilvossius can be identified by their relatively short eyestalks (giving them their 'short-browed' common name) and their specialized digging claws that are perfectly adapted for excavating burrows in soft substrates.
children.funFact: A single mud shrimp can move up to 10 times its body weight in sediment each day while maintaining its elaborate burrow system, making them important ecosystem engineers that help oxygenate seafloor sediments.

children.description: Ghost shrimps are burrowing crustaceans that live in sandy and muddy ocean bottoms, where they dig extensive tunnel systems. These small, pale-colored creatures are rarely seen above ground, earning their 'ghost' name from their elusive nature and translucent appearance. They play an important role in marine ecosystems by aerating sediments through their constant digging.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ghost shrimps have flattened, spade-like claws perfectly adapted for digging, and their bodies are typically pale or translucent. Unlike many other shrimp families, they spend almost their entire lives underground in burrow systems rather than swimming freely.
children.funFact: A single ghost shrimp can move up to 24 times its own body weight in sediment each day while maintaining its elaborate burrow system, making them some of the ocean's most industrious engineers.

children.name: Lithodidae
Lithodes
children.description: Lithodes is a genus of large, spiny king crabs found in cold northern waters. These impressive crustaceans are characterized by their massive size, heavily armored shells, and long, powerful legs that make them formidable deep-water predators and scavengers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lithodes crabs are distinguished from other king crabs by their extremely spiny carapace covered in sharp projections and their particularly robust, heavily calcified shells that provide exceptional protection.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'crabs,' king crabs in the genus Lithodes are actually more closely related to hermit crabs and have evolved their crab-like appearance independently through a process called convergent evolution.

children.description: King crabs are large, heavily armored crabs known for their impressive size and distinctive asymmetrical abdomens that they tuck under their bodies. These fascinating crustaceans are actually more closely related to hermit crabs than to true crabs, representing an evolutionary example of carcinization - the process by which non-crab crustaceans evolve crab-like features.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true crabs, king crabs have only three pairs of walking legs visible (the fourth pair is hidden and used for cleaning gills), and their abdomens are asymmetrical and folded under their bodies rather than being symmetrically flattened.
children.funFact: Despite their name and crab-like appearance, king crabs evolved from hermit crab ancestors and still retain the asymmetrical abdomen of their shell-dwelling relatives.

children.name: Laomediidae
Naushonia
children.description: Naushonia is a genus of small marine crustaceans that belong to the mud shrimp family. These burrowing creatures live in soft sediments along the coast, where they dig elaborate tunnel systems in the mud and sand.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Naushonia can be distinguished from other mud shrimps by their distinctive body proportions and the specific arrangement of their appendages, particularly their specialized digging claws.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'shrimp,' these creatures are more closely related to lobsters and spend most of their lives hidden underground in their burrow networks.

children.description: Laomediidae is a small family of marine hydrozoans, which are simple colonial animals related to jellyfish and corals. These tiny creatures live attached to surfaces in shallow ocean waters, forming delicate branching colonies that look somewhat like miniature underwater plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their unique colony structure and the specific arrangement of their feeding polyps, which differ from other hydrozoan families in their branching patterns and reproductive structures.
children.funFact: Despite being related to jellyfish, Laomediidae spend their entire lives attached to rocks, shells, or seaweed on the ocean floor and never swim freely through the water.

children.description: Decapods are crustaceans that all share one key feature: they have exactly ten legs (five pairs), which is what their name means in Greek. This diverse group includes all the crabs, lobsters, crayfish, and shrimp you might encounter along New England's coasts and in its freshwater streams and ponds. Despite their varied appearances, from tiny pea crabs to massive lobsters, they all follow this same basic ten-legged body plan.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other crustaceans, decapods always have exactly ten walking legs, and their first pair is often modified into large claws or pincers. They also have well-developed eyes on stalks and complex mouthparts for processing food.
children.funFact: Some decapods are master recyclers - hermit crabs spend their lives moving between empty shells as they grow, while many crabs and lobsters eat their own shed exoskeletons to reclaim valuable calcium and other minerals.

children.name: Isopoda
Idoteidae
Idotea
children.description: Idotea is a genus of marine isopods (pill bug relatives) that live in shallow coastal waters and estuaries. These flattened, elongated crustaceans are excellent swimmers that spend their lives clinging to seaweed, eelgrass, and other marine vegetation where they graze on algae and decaying plant matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other isopods that are more rounded, Idotea species have distinctly flattened, streamlined bodies that are well-adapted for swimming. They also have a characteristic pointed tail segment (telson) that helps distinguish them from other marine isopod genera.
children.funFact: These remarkable isopods can change color to match their surroundings, shifting from green when on seaweed to brown when on different substrates, making them masters of marine camouflage.

children.name: Edotia
children.description: Edotia is a genus of small marine isopods, which are crustaceans related to pill bugs and roly-polies. These flattened, segmented creatures live on the ocean floor in shallow coastal waters, where they crawl along sandy and muddy bottoms feeding on organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Edotia have distinctively flattened, oval-shaped bodies with prominent lobes or projections along their sides, giving them a somewhat leaf-like appearance that helps them blend in with debris on the seafloor.
children.funFact: Despite being marine animals, Edotia isopods are closely related to the familiar terrestrial pill bugs you might find under rocks in your backyard - they're all part of the same order of crustaceans!

children.name: Erichsonella
children.description: Erichsonella is a genus of marine isopods, which are small crustaceans related to pill bugs but adapted for life in the ocean. These flattened, segmented creatures crawl along the seafloor and among marine vegetation, using their seven pairs of legs to navigate their underwater world.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus have elongated, narrow bodies that taper toward the rear, giving them a distinctive streamlined appearance compared to their rounder terrestrial pill bug relatives.
children.funFact: Despite being marine creatures, these isopods are actually more closely related to the common pill bugs you might find in your garden than to most other sea life!

children.name: Synidotea
children.description: Synidotea is a genus of marine isopods, which are small crustaceans related to pill bugs but adapted for life in the ocean. These flattened, segmented creatures crawl along the seafloor and among seaweeds in shallow coastal waters. They are scavengers and detritus feeders, helping to break down organic matter in marine ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Synidotea are distinguished by their elongated, flattened bodies and notably broad tail section (called a pleotelson). They have seven pairs of walking legs and can be identified by their distinctive body proportions compared to other marine isopods.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'Broad-tailed Sevenbits,' these isopods actually have fourteen legs total - seven pairs of walking legs that give them their common name!

children.description: Common Valvetails are marine isopods (relatives of pill bugs) that live in coastal waters and tidal zones. These flattened, segmented crustaceans are excellent swimmers and crawlers, moving gracefully through seaweed beds and over rocky surfaces in search of algae and detritus to eat.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Valvetails get their name from their distinctive tail end, which has paired flap-like structures (uropods) that can close like valves. Their bodies are typically elongated and streamlined compared to other isopod families.
children.funFact: Some valvetail species can change color to match their surroundings, shifting from green when living among seaweed to brown when hiding among rocks and sediment.

children.name: Porcellionidae
Porcellio
children.description: Porcellio is a genus of terrestrial crustaceans commonly known as woodlice or pill bugs. These small, oval-shaped creatures have segmented bodies with hard, shell-like plates and seven pairs of legs. They are among the few crustaceans that have successfully adapted to life on land, though they still need moist environments to survive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of genus Porcellio can be distinguished from other woodlice by their inability to roll into a complete ball when threatened, unlike their pill bug cousins. They also have distinctive two-part terminal segments on their antennae and lack the ability to fully retract their heads.
children.funFact: Despite living on land, Porcellio woodlice still breathe through gill-like structures and must keep them moist, which is why you'll often find them hiding under logs, rocks, or in damp basements.

children.name: Porcellionides
children.description: Porcellionides is a genus of terrestrial isopods, commonly known as pill bugs or roly-polies, that have adapted to life on land rather than in water like their marine relatives. These small crustaceans are characterized by their segmented, oval-shaped bodies and their ability to roll into a tight ball when threatened. They play important roles as decomposers, feeding on decaying organic matter in soil and leaf litter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Porcellionides can be distinguished from other terrestrial isopods by their distinctive coloration patterns and the specific arrangement of their body segments and appendages. They typically have a more flattened body shape compared to some other pill bug genera.
children.funFact: The Powder Blue Isopod gets its name from its striking blue-gray coloration with white mottling, making it one of the most colorful terrestrial isopods in New England.

children.description: Porcellionid woodlice are small, armored crustaceans that have adapted to life on land, though they still need moist environments to survive. These pill bug relatives have segmented, oval-shaped bodies covered in hard plates and can often be found under logs, rocks, and in leaf litter where they feed on decaying organic matter. Unlike their ocean-dwelling cousins, these terrestrial crustaceans breathe through modified gills that work like primitive lungs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Porcellionid woodlice can be distinguished from other woodlouse families by their inability to roll into a complete ball when threatened, unlike pill bugs. They have distinctive triangular tail segments and their antennae have two main sections rather than multiple segments.
children.funFact: Despite being crustaceans more closely related to lobsters and crabs than to insects, porcellionid woodlice are among the few crustaceans that have successfully colonized terrestrial environments, though they still carry their eggs in a water-filled pouch to keep them moist.

children.name: Trichoniscidae
Hyloniscus
children.description: Hyloniscus is a genus of terrestrial isopods, commonly known as woodlice or pill bugs, that have adapted to life in moist woodland environments. These small crustaceans are characterized by their ability to roll into a ball when threatened and their preference for areas near water sources. They play an important role in forest ecosystems by decomposing organic matter like fallen leaves and decaying wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hyloniscus woodlice are distinguished from other terrestrial isopods by their strong association with riparian (waterside) habitats and their particular body proportions and surface textures. They tend to be more elongated than typical pill bugs and have specialized adaptations for living in the moist transition zones between aquatic and terrestrial environments.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'woodlice,' these creatures are actually more closely related to lobsters and crabs than to any insect, as they belong to the crustacean family that colonized land millions of years ago.

children.name: Haplophthalmus
children.description: Haplophthalmus is a genus of small terrestrial isopods, commonly known as pillbugs or woodlice, that live in soil and leaf litter. These tiny crustaceans are important decomposers that help break down organic matter in forest ecosystems. They have segmented bodies and can often roll into a ball when threatened.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their unique eye structure (having simple rather than compound eyes) and specific arrangements of their body segments and appendages that differ from other pillbug genera.
children.funFact: Despite being crustaceans like lobsters and crabs, Haplophthalmus species have successfully adapted to life on land and can be found crawling through the forest floor rather than swimming in water.

children.name: Trichoniscus
children.description: Trichoniscus is a genus of tiny terrestrial isopods, commonly known as pygmy woodlice or pill bugs. These miniature crustaceans are among the smallest members of the woodlouse family, typically measuring just a few millimeters in length. They live in moist soil, leaf litter, and other humid terrestrial environments where they feed on decaying organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their extremely small size and inability to roll into a complete ball like some other woodlice. They have a more elongated body shape compared to their larger pill bug relatives.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'woodlice,' these creatures are actually more closely related to shrimp and lobsters than to any insect, as they belong to the crustacean group that successfully made the transition from sea to land.

children.description: Trichoniscidae is a family of small terrestrial isopods, commonly known as woodlice or pill bugs, that live in moist environments like leaf litter, under logs, and in soil. These tiny crustaceans have segmented bodies and seven pairs of legs, and they play important roles in decomposing organic matter in forest ecosystems. Unlike their marine relatives, they have adapted to life on land while still requiring humid conditions to survive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are typically smaller and more elongated than other woodlice families, and they cannot roll into a complete ball like pill bugs in the family Armadillidiidae. They also tend to be found in deeper soil layers and more hidden microhabitats compared to other terrestrial isopods.
children.funFact: Despite being land-dwellers, these little creatures still breathe through gill-like structures and must keep them moist, which is why you'll often find them scurrying away when you lift up a damp log or pile of leaves.

children.name: Cymothoidae
Livoneca
children.description: Livoneca is a genus of parasitic isopods (marine pill bugs) that live inside the mouths of fish. These crustaceans attach themselves to their host's tongue and feed on blood and mucus, eventually replacing the tongue's function.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other isopods that live freely or on the outside of hosts, Livoneca species specifically inhabit the buccal cavity (mouth) of fish and have specialized hooks and claws for attachment.
children.funFact: Livoneca parasites essentially become their host fish's new tongue, helping the fish manipulate food while continuing to feed on the fish's blood and tissue fluids.

children.name: Nerocila
children.description: Nerocila is a genus of parasitic isopods (marine crustaceans) that live as external parasites on fish. These small, flattened creatures attach themselves to their fish hosts and feed on blood and body fluids. They are part of the cymothoid family, which includes various fish parasites found in marine environments.
