children.distinguishingFeatures: Nerocila species can be distinguished from other fish parasites by their oval, flattened body shape and their ability to attach firmly to the exterior of fish using strong, hooked legs called pereopods.
children.funFact: Despite being parasites, Nerocila don't typically kill their fish hosts - instead, they maintain a long-term relationship that allows both the parasite and host to survive, though the fish may experience reduced swimming ability and energy.

children.name: Olencira
children.description: Olencira is a genus of predatory true bugs that are specialized hunters in aquatic environments. These insects are part of the water boatman family and are skilled swimmers that actively pursue their prey underwater rather than waiting in ambush.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many aquatic bugs that are scavengers or ambush predators, Olencira species are active hunters that chase down their prey while swimming. They have a more streamlined body shape compared to their relatives, which helps them move efficiently through the water.
children.funFact: The name 'praegustator' means 'taster' in Latin, referring to this bug's habit of sampling potential prey before deciding whether to make a full attack.

children.description: Fish isopods are parasitic crustaceans that live on or inside fish, where they feed on blood, mucus, or tissue from their hosts. These flattened, oval-shaped creatures are related to pill bugs but have adapted to an aquatic lifestyle attached to fish. They have strong claws and hooks that help them grip onto their fishy hosts.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike free-living isopods, fish isopods have specialized attachment structures and mouthparts designed for parasitism. They also show extreme sexual dimorphism, with females often much larger than males.
children.funFact: Some fish isopods actually replace their host's tongue - the parasite attaches to the base of the fish's tongue until the tongue falls off, then the isopod functions as a living replacement tongue!

children.name: Armadillidiidae
Armadillidium
children.description: Pillbugs are small, gray, oval-shaped crustaceans that live on land and are famous for their ability to roll into a perfect ball when threatened. Despite their common name, they're not actually bugs at all, but rather terrestrial relatives of shrimp and crabs that breathe through modified gills. They're commonly found under logs, rocks, and in other damp places where they feed on decaying plant matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other woodlice, true pillbugs can completely roll themselves into a tight ball, protecting their soft undersides with their hard, segmented shell. This defensive behavior is what gives them their distinctive 'pill' name.
children.funFact: Pillbugs are one of the few crustaceans that have successfully made the transition from ocean to land, but they still need moisture to breathe through their gill-like structures.

children.description: Pill woodlice are terrestrial crustaceans that have evolved the remarkable ability to roll into a perfect ball when threatened, earning them the common name 'pillbugs' or 'roly-polies.' These small, segmented creatures have hard, armor-like shells made of overlapping plates that protect their soft bodies. Despite living on land, they still breathe through gills and need moist environments to survive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other woodlice families, pill woodlice can completely roll themselves into a tight, spherical ball with no body parts visible. This defensive rolling ability is made possible by their highly flexible, articulated shell segments.
children.funFact: Pill woodlice are more closely related to shrimp and lobsters than to insects, making them one of the few crustaceans that have successfully adapted to life on land!

children.name: Trachelipodidae
Trachelipus
children.description: Trachelipus is a genus of terrestrial isopods, commonly known as woodlice or pill bugs, that have adapted to life on land. These small crustaceans have segmented, armored bodies and can roll into a ball when threatened. They breathe through modified gills and need moist environments to survive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Trachelipus can be distinguished from other woodlice by their ability to roll into a complete sphere and their distinctive body proportions with a relatively narrow head region.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'bugs,' Trachelipus woodlice are actually more closely related to shrimp and lobsters than to insects, making them one of the few crustaceans that have successfully colonized terrestrial habitats.

children.name: Nagurus
children.description: Nagurus is a small genus of terrestrial isopods, commonly known as woodlice or pill bugs, that are adapted to life on land rather than in water like their marine relatives. These small crustaceans have segmented, armored bodies and are important decomposers in forest ecosystems, feeding on decaying organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Nagurus are characterized by their distinctively small size and gray coloration with striped patterns, setting them apart from the more common larger woodlice found in New England.
children.funFact: Despite being crustaceans like lobsters and crabs, Nagurus woodlice have successfully adapted to terrestrial life and can be found under logs and leaf litter in forests throughout the region.

children.description: Trachelipodid woodlice are terrestrial crustaceans that have adapted to life on land, though they still need moist environments to survive. These small, segmented creatures are part of the larger group of animals commonly called pill bugs, roly-polies, or sowbugs. They play important ecological roles as decomposers, feeding on decaying plant material and helping to recycle nutrients in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their ability to partially roll into a ball when threatened, though not as completely as some other woodlice families. They have distinctive respiratory structures and specific arrangements of their body segments that set them apart from other woodlice groups.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'bugs,' these creatures are actually more closely related to shrimp and lobsters than to insects, as they are crustaceans that evolved to live on land!

children.name: Ligiidae
children.commonName: Rock Lice, Sea Slaters, and Allies

children.name: Ligia
children.description: Sea slaters are marine isopods that look like large, flattened pill bugs or roly-polies but live along rocky coastlines and harbor areas. These hardy crustaceans scurry quickly across rocks, docks, and seawalls, feeding on decaying organic matter and algae. They're essentially the ocean's cleanup crew, playing an important role in breaking down dead plant and animal material along the shore.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their terrestrial pill bug cousins, sea slaters cannot roll into a ball and are much larger and faster-moving. They have long antennae and are excellent climbers that can quickly disappear into rock crevices when disturbed.
children.funFact: Sea slaters can survive both underwater and on land by using modified gills that work like primitive lungs, allowing them to breathe air while staying moist.

children.description: Ligiidae are terrestrial and semi-aquatic isopods that have adapted to life on land while maintaining close ties to marine environments. These flattened, segmented crustaceans are commonly found along rocky coastlines, under driftwood, and in other moist coastal habitats where they feed on decaying organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other terrestrial isopods, members of Ligiidae have well-developed eyes and are excellent runners, capable of quickly scurrying across rocks and sand when disturbed. They also retain the ability to swim, which sets them apart from pill bugs and other fully terrestrial relatives.
children.funFact: Sea slaters can actually survive underwater for extended periods and are often found in the splash zone of rocky shores, making them one of the few crustaceans that successfully bridge the gap between marine and terrestrial life.

children.name: Oniscidae
Oniscus
children.description: Oniscus is a genus of terrestrial crustaceans commonly known as woodlice or pill bugs. These small, oval-shaped creatures have segmented bodies covered in hard, shiny plates that help protect them from drying out. They are among the few crustaceans that have successfully adapted to life on land, though they still need moist environments to survive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Oniscus are characterized by their particularly shiny, smooth exoskeleton and their inability to roll into a complete ball when threatened, unlike some other woodlice. They have two pairs of lungs and can be identified by their distinctive segmented antennae.
children.funFact: Despite being land-dwellers, Oniscus woodlice still breathe through gill-like structures and must keep them moist, which is why you'll often find them hiding under rocks, logs, or in other damp places during the day.

children.description: Sow bugs are terrestrial crustaceans that have adapted to life on land, though they still need moist environments to survive. They are oval-shaped, segmented creatures with seven pairs of legs and the ability to roll into a tight ball when threatened. Despite being called 'bugs,' they're actually more closely related to shrimp and lobsters than to insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of the Oniscidae family can be distinguished from other terrestrial isopods by their ability to roll completely into a perfect sphere when disturbed. They also have a smoother, more polished appearance compared to other sow bug families.
children.funFact: Sow bugs are one of the few crustacean groups that have successfully colonized land, and they actually help improve soil quality by breaking down dead plant material and recycling nutrients back into the ecosystem.

children.name: Philosciidae
Philoscia
children.description: Philoscia is a genus of terrestrial isopods, commonly known as woodlice or pill bugs, that live in moist environments under logs, stones, and leaf litter. These small, segmented crustaceans have oval-shaped bodies with seven pairs of legs and breathe through gill-like structures that must stay moist. They play an important role in forest ecosystems by breaking down decaying organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Philoscia woodlice are distinguished from other woodlouse genera by their distinctive striped patterns and their inability to roll into a complete ball when threatened, unlike pill bugs (Armadillidium).
children.funFact: Despite being crustaceans more closely related to lobsters and crabs, Philoscia woodlice have successfully adapted to life on land, though they still need moisture to breathe and will quickly dry out in direct sunlight.

children.description: Philosciid woodlice are small, terrestrial crustaceans that have adapted to life on land, though they still need moist environments to survive. These oval-shaped creatures can roll into a ball when threatened and feed primarily on decaying plant matter, making them important decomposers in forest ecosystems. They breathe through gill-like structures that must stay damp, which is why you'll often find them under logs, rocks, or leaf litter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other woodlouse families, philosciids have a distinctive ability to roll into a perfect sphere and typically have smoother, more rounded body segments. They also tend to be smaller and more agile than many of their woodlouse relatives.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'woodlice,' these creatures are actually more closely related to shrimp and lobsters than to any true lice or insects!

children.name: Halophilosciidae
Littorophiloscia
children.description: Littorophiloscia is a specialized genus of woodlice that have adapted to life in coastal saltmarsh environments. These small crustaceans are uniquely equipped to handle the challenging conditions of tidal zones where saltwater regularly floods their habitat.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical terrestrial woodlice, members of this genus have evolved special physiological adaptations that allow them to tolerate high salt concentrations and periodic submersion in seawater.
children.funFact: Despite being crustaceans related to lobsters and crabs, these saltmarsh woodlice can actually survive underwater for extended periods during high tides, essentially 'holding their breath' until the water recedes.

children.description: Halophilosciidae is a small family of terrestrial isopods (commonly called pill bugs or roly-polies) that have adapted to live in coastal environments. These small crustaceans are specially equipped to handle the salty conditions found near shorelines, making them one of the few pill bug families that can thrive in marine-influenced habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most terrestrial isopods that avoid salty conditions, members of this family have evolved physiological adaptations that allow them to tolerate high salt concentrations in their environment.
children.funFact: Despite being crustaceans like crabs and lobsters, these coastal pill bugs have successfully made the transition from sea to land while still maintaining their connection to salty environments.

children.name: Cylisticidae
Cylisticus
children.description: Cylisticus is a genus of terrestrial isopods, commonly known as woodlice or pill bugs, that have adapted to life on land rather than in water like their marine relatives. These small crustaceans are characterized by their ability to roll into a tight ball when threatened, which helps protect their soft underside from predators and prevents water loss.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Cylisticus can be distinguished from other woodlice by their highly convex, dome-shaped body and their exceptional ability to form a perfect sphere when rolling up, earning them the nickname 'pill bugs.'
children.funFact: Despite being crustaceans more closely related to shrimp and lobsters, Cylisticus woodlice have successfully colonized terrestrial environments and can actually drown if submerged in water for too long.

children.description: Cylisticid woodlice are small, oval-shaped crustaceans that have adapted to life on land, though they still need moisture to survive. They are part of the larger group of pill bugs and sow bugs that you might find under logs, rocks, or in leaf litter. Like their relatives, they breathe through gill-like structures and play an important role in decomposing organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cylisticid woodlice can be distinguished from other woodlouse families by their ability to roll into a complete ball when threatened, and by specific details of their body segmentation and antennae structure.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'bugs,' woodlice are actually more closely related to shrimp and lobsters than to insects, making them one of the few successful crustacean groups to colonize dry land.

children.name: Asellidae
Conasellus
children.description: American Waterslaters are small, flattened crustaceans that live in freshwater environments like springs, caves, and groundwater. They are related to terrestrial pill bugs and sowbugs, but have adapted to life in aquatic habitats. These tiny creatures typically measure just a few millimeters long and have segmented bodies with multiple pairs of legs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their land-dwelling relatives, waterslaters have gills adapted for breathing underwater and are typically more elongated and flattened. They lack the ability to roll into a ball like many terrestrial isopods.
children.funFact: Waterslaters are often found in cave systems and underground waters, making them part of the hidden aquatic world that exists beneath our feet throughout New England.

children.description: Freshwater isopods in the family Asellidae are small, flattened crustaceans that have adapted to life in freshwater environments like streams, ponds, and groundwater. These aquatic relatives of pill bugs have segmented bodies with seven pairs of legs and breathe through gills, spending their entire lives underwater. They are important decomposers that help break down dead plant material and organic matter in aquatic ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their terrestrial pill bug cousins, Asellidae cannot roll into a ball and have gills adapted for extracting oxygen from water rather than air. They also tend to be more elongated and flattened than land-dwelling isopods.
children.funFact: Some freshwater isopods can live for several years and are excellent indicators of water quality - their presence often signals clean, well-oxygenated water.

children.name: Detonidae
Armadilloniscus
children.description: Driftclingers are small, pill bug-like crustaceans that live along rocky coastlines and sandy beaches. Unlike their terrestrial cousins, these marine isopods have adapted to life in the harsh intertidal zone where they cling to driftwood, seaweed, and other debris washed up by the waves.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Driftclingers can be distinguished from terrestrial pill bugs by their flattened, more oval-shaped bodies and their ability to survive in saltwater environments. They have specialized claws and body segments that help them grip onto smooth, wet surfaces.
children.funFact: Despite being crustaceans like lobsters and crabs, driftclingers can roll into a perfect ball when threatened, just like their land-dwelling pill bug relatives!

children.description: Detonidae is a small family of terrestrial isopods, commonly known as pill bugs or roly-polies, that have adapted to live in coastal environments. These tiny crustaceans are characterized by their ability to cling to rocks and other surfaces in areas where freshwater meets saltwater, such as tidal zones and stream mouths.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most terrestrial isopods that prefer moist soil or leaf litter, members of Detonidae are specialized for life on rocky surfaces near water. They have enhanced gripping abilities that allow them to maintain their hold on surfaces even when splashed by waves or strong currents.
children.funFact: The common name 'driftclingers' perfectly describes their lifestyle - they can hang onto rocks and driftwood so tenaciously that they rarely get washed away even during high tide or flooding.

children.name: Anthuridae
Cyathura
children.description: Cyathura is a genus of small, elongated marine isopods that live in brackish and saltwater environments. These tiny crustaceans are found burrowing in soft sediments like mud and sand in estuaries, salt marshes, and shallow coastal waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Cyathura can be distinguished from other isopods by their cylindrical, worm-like body shape and their specialized burrowing lifestyle in marine sediments.
children.funFact: Despite being crustaceans related to pill bugs, Cyathura species have evolved such a worm-like appearance that they were originally mistaken for marine worms by early naturalists.

children.description: Anthuridae is a family of small, marine crustaceans known as isopods that live in shallow coastal waters and estuaries. These flattened, segmented creatures are specialized for life in sandy and muddy bottoms where they burrow and feed on organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family have elongated, cylindrical bodies with a distinctive pointed tail section (pleotelson) and specialized burrowing appendages that help them move through sediment.
children.funFact: Despite being crustaceans related to lobsters and crabs, anthurids look more like tiny underwater pillbugs and can quickly disappear into sand when disturbed.

children.name: Platyarthridae
Platyarthrus
children.description: Platyarthrus is a genus of tiny, pale woodlice that have evolved to live exclusively with ants in their nests. These small crustaceans are completely dependent on ant colonies for survival, living as uninvited but tolerated guests in the underground world of their hosts. Unlike their garden-dwelling cousins, members of this genus have adapted to a life of darkness and close association with social insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These woodlice are distinguished from other terrestrial isopods by their extremely small size, pale coloration, and complete dependence on ant colonies for habitat. They lack the ability to survive outside of ant nests and have evolved specialized behaviors to avoid being attacked by their hosts.
children.funFact: Ant woodlice are so specialized for life with ants that they've lost the ability to roll into a ball like many other woodlice, instead relying on their ant hosts' protection and mimicking ant pheromones to avoid being treated as intruders.

children.description: Platyarthrid woodlice are tiny, pale crustaceans that have adapted to life on land rather than in water like their marine relatives. These small arthropods are characterized by their flattened, segmented bodies and their ability to roll into a ball when threatened, though they're much smaller than the common pill bugs most people know.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other woodlice families, platyarthrids are typically very small (usually under 5mm) and often have a more delicate, less armored appearance. They tend to be found in specialized microhabitats rather than the general soil and leaf litter where larger woodlice live.
children.funFact: Many platyarthrid woodlice are found living in ant nests, where they benefit from the ants' protection and stable environment without harming their hosts.

children.name: Janiridae
Jaera
children.description: Jaera is a genus of tiny marine isopods (pill bug relatives) that live in rocky intertidal zones along coastlines. These small crustaceans are flattened and oval-shaped, typically measuring just a few millimeters long, and they crawl around on rocks and in crevices where they feed on algae and organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Jaera species are distinguished from other marine isopods by their extremely small size, distinctive body proportions, and their preference for high intertidal rocky habitats where they can tolerate significant exposure to air during low tides.
children.funFact: Despite being less than 5mm long, Jaera isopods are remarkably hardy and can survive being completely out of water for hours during low tide by hiding in moist rock crevices.

children.description: Janiridae are tiny marine isopods (pill bug relatives) that live in coastal waters and tidal zones. These small crustaceans have flattened, oval-shaped bodies and are typically found crawling among seaweed, under rocks, or in shallow water sediments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their terrestrial pill bug cousins, janirids are exclusively marine and have specialized gills for underwater breathing. They have distinctively flattened bodies that are wider than they are tall, making them well-suited for squeezing into tight spaces between rocks and algae.
children.funFact: Despite being related to the familiar pill bugs found in gardens, these marine janirids cannot roll into a ball and instead rely on their flat profile to hide in crevices when threatened.

children.name: Bopyridae
Probopyrus
children.description: Probopyrus is a genus of parasitic isopods (related to pill bugs and roly-polies) that live inside the gill chambers of shrimp and other crustaceans. These small, flattened creatures attach themselves to their hosts and feed on their body fluids. They're part of a specialized group of marine parasites that have adapted to life inside other sea creatures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Probopyrus can be distinguished from other parasitic isopods by their specific adaptation to living in the gill chambers of decapod crustaceans like shrimp. They have a distinctive flattened, asymmetrical body shape that helps them fit snugly against their host's gills.
children.funFact: Female Probopyrus are much larger than males and can actually cause visible swelling on one side of their shrimp host's body, creating a noticeable bulge in the gill chamber area.

children.description: Decapod ectoparasitic isopods are small crustaceans that live as external parasites on other crustaceans like crabs, shrimp, and crayfish. They attach themselves to their hosts and feed on their body fluids, often causing noticeable swelling or bulges on the host's body. These parasites have flattened, segmented bodies that are well-adapted for clinging to their hosts.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike free-living isopods, these species have specialized claws and body shapes specifically designed for gripping onto and living on other crustaceans. They also show extreme sexual dimorphism, with females being much larger than males and often losing many typical isopod features as they mature into their parasitic lifestyle.
children.funFact: Female bopyrid isopods can grow so large on their hosts that they actually cause the host's shell to bulge outward, creating a visible bump that makes infected crabs and shrimp easy to spot!

children.name: Sphaeromatidae
Sphaeroma
children.description: Sphaeroma is a genus of small marine crustaceans commonly known as seapills or pill bugs of the sea. These isopods have the remarkable ability to roll into a tight ball when threatened, much like their terrestrial pill bug relatives. They are typically found in shallow coastal waters, living among rocks, seaweed, and other marine debris.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Sphaeroma can be distinguished from other marine isopods by their ability to completely roll into a smooth, ball-like shape and their relatively rounded body form when extended.
children.funFact: Despite being marine creatures, seapills are closely related to the familiar terrestrial pill bugs (roly-polies) found in gardens, and both groups evolved the same defensive ball-rolling behavior independently.

children.description: Typical seapills are small, oval-shaped marine crustaceans that live in shallow coastal waters and can roll into a tight ball when threatened, much like terrestrial pill bugs. They are part of the isopod group, which makes them relatives of sowbugs and roly-polies, but these species have adapted to life in saltwater environments. These hardy little creatures are commonly found under rocks, in seaweed, and among marine debris in the intertidal zone.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other marine isopods, seapills have a distinctly rounded, dome-shaped body that allows them to roll into a perfect sphere for protection. Their ability to completely enclose themselves by tucking their head, legs, and antennae inside their shell-like body segments sets them apart from their flatter, more elongated isopod relatives.
children.funFact: When a seapill rolls into a ball, it can survive being tumbled around by waves and even brief periods out of water, making it one of the most resilient creatures in the rocky intertidal zone.

children.name: Ancinidae
Ancinus
children.description: Ancinus is a genus of terrestrial isopods, commonly known as pillbugs or roly-polies, that are found in woodland habitats. These small crustaceans have adapted to life on land and play an important role in breaking down decaying organic matter in forest ecosystems. Like other pillbugs, they have segmented bodies and can roll into a ball when threatened.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Ancinus are notably flattened compared to other pillbug genera, giving them their common name of 'flat pillbugs.' This compressed body shape helps them squeeze into tight spaces under logs, rocks, and leaf litter.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'bugs,' flat pillbugs are actually more closely related to lobsters and shrimp than to insects, as they belong to the crustacean family.

children.description: Spikepills are tiny terrestrial isopods (pill bugs or roly-polies) that belong to a small family found primarily in soil and leaf litter. These miniature crustaceans are among the smallest pill bugs, typically measuring just a few millimeters in length. Like their larger cousins, they can roll into a ball when threatened, but their diminutive size makes them easy to overlook.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Spikepills are distinguished from other pill bug families by their extremely small size and the presence of distinctive spines or tubercles on their exoskeleton. They also have unique arrangements of their body segments that differ from common pill bugs found in gardens.
children.funFact: Despite being crustaceans more closely related to shrimp and lobsters, spikepills have successfully adapted to life on land and can survive in remarkably dry conditions for such tiny creatures.

children.name: Chaetiliidae
Chiridotea
children.description: Sandmoles are small marine crustaceans that live buried in sandy ocean bottoms along the coast. These tiny creatures are actually isopods, related to pill bugs and roly-polies, but have adapted to life burrowing through underwater sand rather than living on land.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their terrestrial pill bug relatives, sandmoles have flattened, streamlined bodies perfectly shaped for moving through sand, and specialized swimming legs called pleopods for moving through water.
children.funFact: Despite their name, sandmoles aren't moles at all - they're actually more closely related to the pill bugs you might find in your garden!

children.description: Chaetiliidae is a small family of marine isopods, which are crustaceans related to pill bugs and sowbugs. These aquatic creatures are commonly known as sandmoles because they burrow through sandy and muddy sediments on the ocean floor. They have flattened, segmented bodies that are well-adapted for their burrowing lifestyle.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their terrestrial pill bug relatives, sandmoles have specialized swimming appendages and gills for underwater life. Their bodies are more elongated and streamlined compared to the rounded shape of land-dwelling isopods.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'sandmoles,' these creatures are actually more closely related to shrimp and crabs than to actual moles, and they use their powerful legs to 'swim' through sand much like moles move through soil.

children.description: Isopods are a diverse group of crustaceans that includes familiar pill bugs and sow bugs found in gardens, as well as marine and freshwater species. All isopods have flattened bodies from top to bottom and seven pairs of similar-looking legs, which gives them their name meaning 'equal feet.' They range from terrestrial woodlice that roll into balls when threatened to aquatic species and even parasites that live on fish.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Isopods can be distinguished from other crustaceans by their dorsoventrally flattened bodies, seven pairs of walking legs that are all similar in appearance, and their segmented bodies with overlapping plates. Unlike other crustaceans, many terrestrial isopods have adapted to life on land and can roll into a protective ball.
children.funFact: Some terrestrial isopods like pill bugs are actually more closely related to shrimp and lobsters than to insects, and they still breathe through gill-like structures that must stay moist, which is why you'll find them under logs and rocks.

children.name: Amphipoda
Talitridae
Americorchestia
children.description: Americorchestia is a genus of small crustaceans commonly known as sandhoppers or beach fleas that live along sandy shorelines. These tiny creatures are excellent jumpers that hop around on beaches, using their powerful hind legs to leap impressive distances when disturbed. They play an important role in beach ecosystems by breaking down decaying seaweed and other organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Americorchestia are distinguished from other sandhopper genera by their relatively large eyes and their preference for living in the wrack zone of sandy beaches rather than rocky shores.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'beach fleas,' sandhoppers are actually more closely related to shrimp than to fleas and can jump up to 20 times their own body length!

children.name: Platorchestia
children.description: Platorchestia is a genus of small, shrimp-like crustaceans commonly known as beach hoppers or sand fleas. These terrestrial amphipods live in coastal areas where they burrow in sand and feed on decaying organic matter like seaweed and other beach debris. They are important decomposers in beach ecosystems, helping to break down washed-up materials.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Platorchestia can be distinguished from other beach hopper genera by their flattened body shape and specific arrangements of their antennae and legs. They have particularly well-developed jumping legs that allow them to leap considerable distances when disturbed.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'sand fleas,' these creatures are actually more closely related to shrimp than to fleas, and they can jump up to several times their own body length when trying to escape predators!

children.name: Speziorchestia
children.description: Speziorchestia is a genus of beach hoppers, small crustaceans that are perfectly adapted for life along sandy shorelines. These amphipods are excellent jumpers that can leap several times their body length when disturbed, earning them their common name of beach hoppers or sand fleas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus have specialized legs for jumping and can be distinguished from other beach amphipods by their robust build and specific body proportions. They have large, powerful hind legs that give them their impressive jumping ability.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'sand fleas,' these creatures are actually more closely related to shrimp than to true fleas, and they play an important role as beach cleaners by feeding on decaying seaweed and organic matter washed up on shore.

children.description: Sandhoppers and landhoppers are small, shrimp-like crustaceans that have adapted to life on land and in the intertidal zone. Unlike their marine relatives, these creatures can survive out of water for extended periods and are often found hopping around in beach wrack, under logs, or in moist soil near coastlines. They have laterally compressed bodies that allow them to squeeze into tight spaces and powerful legs for jumping.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets this family apart from other amphipods is their ability to live terrestrially or semi-terrestrially, rather than being fully aquatic. They have specialized gills that can extract oxygen from air when moist, and their jumping behavior is much more pronounced than their swimming cousins.
children.funFact: Despite being crustaceans like lobsters and crabs, some landhoppers can jump up to 20 times their own body length when disturbed, earning them the nickname 'lawn shrimp' when they venture into people's yards during humid nights.

children.name: Gammaridae
Gammarus
children.description: Gammarus is a genus of small, shrimp-like crustaceans called amphipods that live in both freshwater and marine environments throughout New England. These tiny creatures have curved, laterally compressed bodies and swim on their sides, earning them the common name 'scuds.' They're important members of aquatic ecosystems, feeding on decaying organic matter and serving as food for fish and other aquatic animals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Gammarus species are distinguished from other amphipods by their robust build, well-developed gnathopods (grasping appendages), and relatively large size compared to other scuds. They also have distinctive antenna structures and body segments that help identify them in the field.
children.funFact: Despite being only about half an inch long, Gammarus scuds are incredibly strong swimmers and can rapidly dart through the water column by flexing their curved bodies like tiny aquatic springs.

children.description: Gammaridae are small, shrimp-like crustaceans that live in freshwater and marine environments throughout New England. These amphipods have laterally compressed bodies that curve into a distinctive C-shape when disturbed, earning them the common name 'scuds' or 'sideswimmers.' They are important decomposers that feed on decaying plant matter, algae, and organic debris in aquatic ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other amphipod families, Gammaridae have relatively large, well-developed eyes and lack the specialized filtering appendages found in some related groups. Their antennae are typically long and prominent, and they have strong, grasping legs adapted for clinging to vegetation and substrate.
children.funFact: Some Gammarus species can survive being frozen solid in ice during winter and resume normal activity when they thaw out in spring.

children.name: Crangonyctidae
Crangonyx
children.description: Crangonyx is a genus of tiny freshwater amphipods, which are small shrimp-like crustaceans that live in underground waters, springs, and boggy areas. These microscopic creatures are typically found in groundwater systems and are specially adapted to life in dark, aquatic environments. They play important roles as decomposers in freshwater ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their marine amphipod relatives, Crangonyx species are exclusively freshwater dwellers that have evolved to thrive in underground and spring-fed waters. They tend to be smaller and more delicate than surface-dwelling amphipods.
children.funFact: These tiny amphipods are so specialized for their underground habitats that many species are found only in specific local groundwater systems, making them excellent indicators of groundwater health.

children.name: Sicifera
children.description: Sicifera is a genus of small freshwater and brackish water amphipods, which are tiny shrimp-like crustaceans that swim and crawl through aquatic environments. These amphipods are typically found in coastal marshes and swamps where fresh and salt water mix. They play important roles as decomposers, feeding on decaying plant material and organic matter in their wetland habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Sicifera can be distinguished from other amphipods by their specific body proportions and the arrangement of their swimming appendages. They are specially adapted to handle the varying salinity levels found in coastal wetland environments.
children.funFact: The Coastal Swamp Amphipod can survive dramatic changes in water salinity throughout the day as tides bring salt water in and out of their marsh habitats.

children.description: Crangonyctidae is a family of small, shrimp-like freshwater amphipods that live in underground waters like caves, springs, and groundwater systems. These tiny crustaceans are typically pale or white in color and have adapted to life in dark, aquatic environments. They are important members of subterranean ecosystems, feeding on organic matter and serving as food for other cave-dwelling animals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their marine cousins, these amphipods are exclusively freshwater dwellers that have evolved specialized features for underground life, including reduced or absent eyes and often lacking pigmentation. They typically have elongated antennae and modified appendages suited for navigating through groundwater spaces and cave systems.
children.funFact: Many species in this family are essentially living fossils, having evolved in isolated underground water systems for millions of years, making them important indicators of ancient geological and hydrological processes.

children.name: Caprellidae
Caprella
children.description: Caprella is a genus of marine crustaceans commonly known as skeleton shrimp, though they're actually amphipods rather than true shrimp. These bizarre-looking creatures have extremely thin, stick-like bodies that make them appear almost skeletal, which is how they got their common name. They live attached to seaweed, hydroids, and other marine structures where they feed on small particles and plankton.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Skeleton shrimp have dramatically elongated, thin bodies with reduced abdomens and only a few pairs of functional legs, giving them a praying mantis-like appearance. Unlike other amphipods, they lack the typical laterally compressed body shape and instead have a linear form perfectly adapted for clinging to branching structures.
children.funFact: Skeleton shrimp are masters of camouflage - they sway back and forth with water currents while clinging to seaweed, making them nearly impossible to spot until you look closely at marine growth on docks and rocks.

children.description: Skeleton shrimp are bizarre-looking marine amphipods that have evolved extremely thin, stick-like bodies that resemble tiny praying mantises more than typical shrimp. They live attached to seaweeds, hydroids, and other underwater structures, swaying with the currents while using their large front claws to capture small prey and plankton. Despite their name, they're not actually shrimp but are more closely related to beach hoppers and other amphipods.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other amphipods, skeleton shrimp have dramatically elongated, tubular bodies with reduced abdomens and specially modified legs for gripping onto surfaces. Their stick-thin appearance and swaying movements make them almost impossible to spot among the seaweed where they live.
children.funFact: Skeleton shrimp can bend their bodies nearly in half and perform acrobatic movements, sometimes hanging upside down or doing complete somersaults while still clinging to their host with their hind legs.

children.name: Hyalidae
Ptilohyale
children.description: Ptilohyale is a genus of small marine amphipods, which are tiny shrimp-like crustaceans that live in coastal waters. These creatures are part of the diverse world of marine invertebrates that scuttle around in shallow ocean environments, often hiding among seaweed and under rocks.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Ptilohyale are distinguished by their feathery or plume-like appendages (the name literally means 'feathery saltwater creature') and their specialized body structure adapted for life in marine environments.
children.funFact: Despite being only a few millimeters long, these tiny amphipods are important members of marine food webs, serving as food for fish while helping to break down organic matter on the seafloor.

children.name: Apohyale
children.description: Apohyale is a genus of small marine amphipods, which are shrimp-like crustaceans that live in coastal waters. These tiny creatures are part of the diverse world of amphipods that play important roles in marine food webs, serving as food for fish and other marine animals while feeding on detritus and small organisms themselves.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Apohyale are distinguished from other amphipod genera by their specific body segmentation patterns and the structure of their appendages, particularly their gnathopods (specialized feeding and grasping limbs).
children.funFact: Despite being only a few millimeters long, Apohyale amphipods are excellent swimmers and can also burrow in sandy sediments, making them perfectly adapted to life in the dynamic intertidal zone.

children.description: Hyalidae is a family of small marine amphipods, which are shrimp-like crustaceans that live in coastal waters. These tiny creatures are typically found among seaweeds, under rocks, and in tide pools along New England's rocky shores. They are important members of the marine food web, feeding on algae and organic matter while serving as food for fish and other marine animals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their translucent bodies and relatively smooth appearance compared to other amphipod families. They typically have fewer spines and projections on their body segments, giving them a more streamlined look.
children.funFact: Despite their small size (usually less than half an inch long), hyalid amphipods are excellent swimmers and can quickly dart through the water using rapid flexing motions of their curved bodies.

children.name: Cyamidae
Cyamus
children.description: Cyamus is a genus of tiny crustaceans known as whale lice that live exclusively on the skin of whales and dolphins. These flattened, crab-like creatures spend their entire lives clinging to their whale hosts, feeding on dead skin and algae that grows on the whale's surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical amphipods, whale lice have extremely flattened bodies and powerful claws specifically adapted for gripping onto whale skin even in rushing water.
children.funFact: Each whale species tends to host its own specific species of whale lice, and scientists can sometimes identify whale species just by examining the lice found on them!

children.description: Whale lice are small, flattened crustaceans that live exclusively on whales and dolphins as external parasites. These tiny creatures spend their entire lives clinging to their whale hosts, feeding on dead skin and other organic matter on the whale's surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical lice (which are insects), whale lice are actually amphipod crustaceans related to beach hoppers and freshwater scuds. They have powerful, hook-like claws that allow them to grip tightly to whale skin even in rushing ocean currents.
children.funFact: Each whale species typically hosts its own unique species of whale lice, and scientists can sometimes identify which type of whale they're studying just by looking at the lice living on it.

children.name: Ischyroceridae
Jassa
children.description: Jassa is a genus of small marine crustaceans called amphipods that live in shallow coastal waters. These tiny shrimp-like creatures are excellent swimmers and can be found clinging to seaweeds, rocks, and other underwater surfaces in tide pools and harbors.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Jassa are distinguished by their enlarged second pair of legs (gnathopods) which have distinctive claw-like structures used for grasping and feeding.
children.funFact: Despite being only about half an inch long, Jassa amphipods are voracious filter feeders that help keep coastal waters clean by consuming algae and organic particles.

children.description: Ischyroceridae is a family of small marine amphipod crustaceans that are commonly found in coastal waters and estuaries. These tiny shrimp-like creatures are excellent swimmers and are often found clinging to seaweed, rocks, and other underwater surfaces. They play important roles in marine food webs as both grazers of algae and prey for fish and other marine animals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their robust, somewhat flattened bodies and strong, well-developed claws (gnathopods) that they use for grasping surfaces and manipulating food. They typically have large eyes and relatively short antennae compared to many other amphipod families.
children.funFact: Some Ischyroceridae amphipods are incredibly abundant in harbors and marinas, where they can form dense populations on dock pilings and boat hulls, sometimes numbering in the thousands per square meter.

children.name: Calliopiidae
Calliopius
children.description: Calliopius is a genus of small marine crustaceans called amphipods that live in cold northern waters. These tiny shrimp-like creatures are excellent swimmers and spend their lives drifting and swimming in the open ocean as part of the plankton community.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their streamlined bodies and powerful swimming abilities, which set them apart from the many amphipod species that crawl along the seafloor or burrow in sediment.
children.funFact: These planktonic amphipods can perform impressive vertical migrations, swimming hundreds of feet up and down in the water column each day to follow their food and avoid predators.

children.description: Calliopiidae is a small family of marine amphipods, which are tiny shrimp-like crustaceans that live in ocean waters. These small creatures are part of the vast group of amphipods that play important roles in marine food webs, serving as food for fish and other marine animals while feeding on organic matter and small organisms themselves.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished from other amphipods by their specific body segmentation patterns and the structure of their appendages, particularly their antennae and legs used for swimming and crawling.
children.funFact: Despite being tiny creatures often less than an inch long, amphipods like those in Calliopiidae are incredibly abundant in marine environments and can be found swimming in huge swarms that help sustain entire ocean ecosystems.

children.name: Gammarellidae
Gammarellus
children.description: Gammarellus is a genus of small marine amphipods, which are tiny shrimp-like crustaceans that live in coastal waters. These small creatures are part of the diverse world of amphipods that play important roles in marine food webs as both predators of even smaller organisms and prey for fish and other marine animals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Gammarellus amphipods are distinguished from other amphipod genera by their specific body proportions and the arrangement of their appendages, particularly the structure of their antennae and the segments of their bodies.
children.funFact: Despite being only a few millimeters long, Gammarellus amphipods are excellent swimmers and can quickly dart through the water using rapid flexing motions of their segmented bodies.

children.description: Gammarellidae is a small family of amphipod crustaceans - tiny shrimp-like creatures that live in marine environments. These small invertebrates are part of the diverse world of amphipods, which are important members of ocean food webs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished from other amphipods by their specific body structure and taxonomic characteristics, though the family contains relatively few species compared to other amphipod groups.
children.funFact: New England has just one species in this entire family, making it quite rare compared to other amphipod families that might have dozens of local species.

children.name: Hyperiidae
Hyperia
children.description: Hyperia is a genus of small marine crustaceans known as hyperiid amphipods that live as parasites on jellyfish and other gelatinous sea creatures. These tiny shrimp-like animals have evolved to spend their lives riding on or inside their jellyfish hosts, feeding on the host's tissues and reproductive materials. They are specialized oceanic hitchhikers that have adapted to life in the open sea.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hyperia amphipods have unusually large, prominent compound eyes that help them locate jellyfish hosts in the open ocean. Unlike most amphipods that live on the seafloor or near shore, these species are adapted for a pelagic lifestyle with a more streamlined body shape.
children.funFact: Hyperia amphipods can actually steer their jellyfish hosts by positioning themselves strategically on the bell, essentially turning their host into a living submarine that they can direct toward food-rich areas of the ocean.

children.description: Hyperiidae is a family of small marine crustaceans called amphipods that live as parasites or associates on jellyfish and other gelatinous sea creatures. These tiny shrimp-like animals have adapted to life in the open ocean, often riding along with their jellyfish hosts as they drift through the water. They have large compound eyes and modified legs that help them cling to their gelatinous homes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other amphipods that live on the seafloor or near shore, hyperiids have enormous eyes relative to their body size and are specifically adapted for life in the open ocean attached to jellyfish.
children.funFact: Some hyperiid amphipods actually hollow out chambers inside jellyfish bells and live completely within their host, essentially turning the jellyfish into a living submarine!

children.name: Uhlorchestiidae
Uhlorchestia
children.description: Uhlorchestia is a genus of small, jumping amphipod crustaceans that live in coastal salt marshes and sandy beach areas. These tiny creatures are specialized for life in the upper intertidal zone, where they hop around like fleas among marsh grasses and beach wrack.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their aquatic amphipod relatives, Uhlorchestia species are semi-terrestrial and can survive out of water for extended periods. They have powerful jumping legs that allow them to leap considerable distances relative to their small size.
children.funFact: Despite being crustaceans like crabs and lobsters, these marsh hoppers can actually drown if submerged in water for too long, having adapted to breathe air through modified gills.

children.description: Uhlorchestiidae is a small family of amphipod crustaceans that are specially adapted to life in sandy beach environments. These tiny shrimp-like creatures are excellent jumpers and diggers, spending their lives hopping across sand dunes and burrowing into the sand during the day.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their marine relatives, these amphipods have evolved to live entirely on land in coastal sandy areas. They have modified gills that can extract moisture from humid air and powerful jumping legs that help them navigate loose sand.
children.funFact: These beach-hoppers can leap distances up to 20 times their own body length, making them some of the most impressive jumpers in the crustacean world!

children.name: Corophiidae
Corophium
children.description: Corophium is a genus of small marine amphipods, which are tiny shrimp-like crustaceans that live in coastal waters. These creatures are tube-dwelling animals that build U-shaped burrows in muddy or sandy sediments along shorelines and estuaries. They play an important role in marine food webs as both filter feeders and prey for fish and birds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other amphipods that swim freely, Corophium species are semi-sedentary and live in permanent burrows they construct in soft sediments. They have specialized antennae and feeding appendages adapted for filter feeding while remaining safely in their tubes.
children.funFact: Corophium can occur in enormous densities of up to 100,000 individuals per square meter in prime mudflat habitat, creating underwater 'cities' of tiny tubes that help stabilize the seafloor sediment.

children.description: Corophiidae is a family of small marine amphipods (tiny shrimp-like crustaceans) that are skilled builders and diggers. These creatures construct tube-like burrows in mud, sand, or among algae, where they live and feed by filtering particles from the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family have notably enlarged second antennae and specialized limbs adapted for digging and tube construction, setting them apart from other amphipod families.
children.funFact: Some Corophiidae species can dramatically alter coastal sediment structure through their extensive burrowing activities, creating complex underground neighborhoods that provide shelter for other small marine creatures.

children.name: Phronimidae
Phronima
children.description: Phronima is a genus of small marine crustaceans known for their unusual parasitic lifestyle. These amphipods take over the bodies of barrel-shaped sea creatures called salps, hollowing them out and using the empty shells as both homes and nurseries for their young.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other amphipods, Phronima has a distinctly barrel-shaped body and large, prominent eyes that help it navigate the open ocean. Its front legs are modified into powerful grasping claws for manipulating its host.
children.funFact: Phronima inspired the design of the alien creature in the movie 'Alien' - both share the eerie habit of using another organism's body as a nursery for their offspring.

children.description: Phronimidae is a family of marine amphipods known as barrel shrimp or hyperiid amphipods that live a unique pelagic lifestyle in the open ocean. These translucent crustaceans are famous for their parasitic relationship with gelatinous marine animals like salps and jellyfish, where they hollow out and inhabit their hosts like living submarines.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other amphipods that typically live on the seafloor or in shallow waters, phronimids are specialized for life in the open ocean with large eyes adapted for the dim pelagic environment and powerful claws for grasping their gelatinous hosts.
children.funFact: The female phronimid's habit of hollowing out and wearing barrel-shaped salps or other gelatinous creatures inspired the barrel-riding aliens in the classic Disney movie '20,000 Leagues Under the Sea.'

children.name: Ampithoidae
Ampithoe
children.description: Ampithoe is a genus of small marine amphipods, which are tiny shrimp-like crustaceans that live in coastal waters. These creatures are excellent swimmers and crawlers, using their flattened bodies to navigate through seaweed and other underwater vegetation. They play important roles in marine food webs as both grazers and prey for larger animals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Ampithoe can be distinguished from other amphipods by their robust, somewhat flattened bodies and their strong gnathopods (specialized feeding appendages) that they use for grasping algae and detritus.
children.funFact: Ampithoe amphipods are sometimes called 'tube-builders' because they construct protective tubes from algae and sediment particles, which they carry around like portable homes.

children.description: Ampithoidae is a family of small marine crustaceans called amphipods that live among seaweeds and other marine vegetation. These tiny creatures have flattened, shrimp-like bodies and are excellent climbers, using their specialized legs to navigate through underwater plant communities.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their ability to build tube-like nests from bits of algae and debris, which they cement together and live inside for protection.
children.funFact: These industrious little architects can construct elaborate multi-chambered homes that they carry with them as they move through their seaweed neighborhoods.

children.name: Phoxocephalidae
Rhepoxynius
children.description: Rhepoxynius is a genus of small marine amphipod crustaceans that live in the sandy and muddy bottoms of coastal waters. These tiny shrimp-like creatures are part of the diverse world of amphipods, which are important members of marine ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by their distinctive body shape and specialized appendages adapted for burrowing in soft sediments. They have elongated bodies with well-developed pleopods for swimming.
children.funFact: Despite being only a few millimeters long, Rhepoxynius amphipods play an important role in marine food webs, serving as food for fish and helping to recycle nutrients in seafloor sediments.

children.description: Phoxocephalidae is a family of marine amphipods, small shrimp-like crustaceans that live in sandy and muddy ocean bottoms. These tiny creatures are excellent burrowers, using their specialized bodies to dig through sediment where they feed on organic matter and small organisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family have distinctively flattened, streamlined bodies and strong, spade-like appendages that make them highly efficient at burrowing through sand and mud.
children.funFact: These amphipods are so well-adapted to their burrowing lifestyle that they can disappear into sandy sediment in just seconds when disturbed, earning them the nickname 'sand hoppers.'

children.name: Haustoriidae
Parahaustorius
children.description: Parahaustorius is a genus of small marine amphipods (tiny shrimp-like crustaceans) that live in sandy beach environments. These microscopic creatures are specialized for life in the spaces between sand grains, where they feed on organic matter and bacteria.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished from other beach amphipods by their elongated body shape and specialized appendages that help them navigate through sandy sediments.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to beachgoers, these tiny crustaceans are essential members of sandy beach ecosystems, helping to break down organic matter and serving as food for larger marine animals.

children.description: Haustoriidae is a family of small marine amphipods (shrimp-like crustaceans) that are specialized for life in sandy beach environments. These tiny creatures are excellent burrowers, spending most of their lives tunneling through wet sand in the intertidal zone where waves meet the shore.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family have specially modified limbs and body segments that make them exceptional sand diggers, with flattened bodies and powerful digging appendages that allow them to quickly disappear into sand when waves recede.
children.funFact: These amphipods can burrow into sand so quickly that they seem to vanish instantly when a wave washes over them, earning them the nickname 'sand fleas' even though they're actually crustaceans, not insects.

children.description: Amphipods are small, shrimp-like crustaceans that are flattened from side to side, giving them a distinctive curved appearance. They're incredibly diverse, living everywhere from sandy beaches and rocky shores to freshwater streams, caves, and even the open ocean. Most are excellent swimmers or jumpers, using their powerful legs to propel themselves through water or across wet surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other small crustaceans, amphipods have bodies that are compressed laterally (flattened from side to side) rather than from top to bottom, and they typically swim or crawl on their sides. They lack the hard carapace that covers the thorax in many other crustaceans like shrimp and crabs.
children.funFact: Some amphipods called 'whale lice' live their entire lives clinging to whales, while others like beach hoppers can leap several times their body length across the sand at night!

children.name: Balanomorpha
Balanidae
Amphibalanus
children.description: Amphibalanus is a genus of acorn barnacles - those cone-shaped, hard-shelled creatures you often see covering rocks, docks, and boat hulls in coastal waters. These marine crustaceans are actually more closely related to crabs and lobsters than to mollusks, despite their shell-like appearance. All members of this genus are filter feeders that cement themselves permanently to hard surfaces and extend feathery feeding appendages to capture tiny organisms from the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Amphibalanus barnacles are distinguished from other barnacle genera by their specific shell plate arrangements and the detailed structure of their cone-shaped tests. They typically have six wall plates forming their characteristic volcano-like shape, with particular patterns of ridges and growth lines that help scientists tell the different species apart.
children.funFact: These barnacles start life as free-swimming larvae that look nothing like their adult forms - they actually swim around like tiny shrimp before eventually finding the perfect spot to glue their heads down permanently and transform into the familiar cone-shaped adults!

children.name: Balanus
children.description: Rock-barnacles are sturdy, cone-shaped crustaceans that cement themselves permanently to rocky shores, pier pilings, and other hard surfaces in marine environments. These filter-feeding animals create distinctive white or grayish calcium carbonate shells with overlapping plates that can completely close to protect the soft animal inside during low tide.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike acorn barnacles which have a more rounded, volcano-like shape, rock-barnacles typically have taller, more cylindrical shells with distinct vertical ridges and plates. They're generally larger and more robust than other barnacle groups found in New England waters.
children.funFact: Rock-barnacles are actually more closely related to crabs and lobsters than to mollusks like clams and mussels, despite their shell-like appearance and sedentary lifestyle.

children.name: Semibalanus
children.description: Semibalanus is a genus of acorn barnacles that includes some of the most common rocky shore inhabitants in the North Atlantic. These marine crustaceans cement themselves permanently to rocks, docks, and other hard surfaces, where they filter feed by extending feathery appendages from their cone-shaped shells.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Semibalanus have relatively large, robust shells with thick walls and are typically found in the mid to high intertidal zone where they can withstand significant wave action.
children.funFact: Despite being permanently glued in place as adults, Semibalanus barnacles start life as free-swimming larvae that can travel great distances on ocean currents before settling down and transforming into their familiar cone-shaped form.

children.description: Balanidae are the true acorn barnacles, small marine crustaceans that cement themselves permanently to rocks, piers, and other hard surfaces in the intertidal zone. They build cone-shaped shells made of overlapping plates that protect their soft bodies inside. When the tide comes in, they open their shells and extend feathery legs to filter plankton and small particles from the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other barnacle families, Balanidae have shells made of six main wall plates that are fused together, creating their characteristic volcano-like shape. They lack the stalks found in goose barnacles and have a more compact, sturdy build than other acorn barnacle families.
children.funFact: Barnacles were once thought to be mollusks like clams, but they're actually crustaceans related to crabs and lobsters - they're basically upside-down shrimp living in a fortress!

children.name: Chthamalidae
Chthamalus
children.description: Chthamalus is a genus of small, cone-shaped barnacles that attach permanently to rocky surfaces in coastal areas. These marine crustaceans build hard, chalky shells made of overlapping plates that protect their soft bodies inside. They filter-feed by extending feathery appendages to catch tiny particles and plankton from the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Chthamalus barnacles are typically smaller and more delicate than other common barnacle genera, with thinner shell walls and a more compressed, flattened appearance. They often prefer higher positions in the intertidal zone compared to their sturdier relatives.
children.funFact: Despite being permanently glued to rocks as adults, Chthamalus barnacles start life as free-swimming larvae that can travel great distances in ocean currents before settling down to find the perfect rock to call home forever.

children.description: Chthamalid barnacles are small, cone-shaped marine crustaceans that cement themselves permanently to rocks, pier pilings, and other hard surfaces in the intertidal zone. These hardy creatures have thick, overlapping shell plates that form a protective fortress around their soft body parts. They feed by opening their shells and extending feathery appendages to filter tiny plankton and organic particles from the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other barnacle families, chthamalids have only four wall plates instead of six, giving them a more compact, streamlined appearance. They also lack the movable door plates (operculum) that some other barnacles use to seal their shells.
children.funFact: These barnacles can survive being completely out of water for hours during low tide by trapping seawater inside their tightly sealed shells, essentially holding their breath until the tide returns.

children.name: Coronulidae
Coronula
children.description: Coronula is a genus of whale barnacles that live exclusively attached to the skin of large whales. These specialized crustaceans have evolved thick, heavy shells and powerful cement glands that allow them to maintain their grip on their massive hosts as they swim through the ocean. Unlike typical barnacles that attach to rocks or ships, these barnacles have formed a unique partnership with marine mammals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Coronula barnacles are distinguished by their unusually thick, robust shells and specialized attachment structures that can penetrate whale skin. They are much larger and more heavily built than most other barnacle species, adapted specifically for life on fast-moving whale hosts.
children.funFact: Coronula barnacles are so tightly bonded to their whale hosts that they often leave permanent scars on the whale's skin, and scientists can use barnacle scars to identify individual whales over many years.

children.description: Whale barnacles are specialized crustaceans that live exclusively attached to the skin of whales and other large marine mammals. Unlike their rock-dwelling cousins, these barnacles have evolved thick, sturdy shells and strong attachment mechanisms to withstand the powerful forces of moving through ocean waters at high speeds. They filter-feed on plankton and small organisms from the water flowing past their whale hosts.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Whale barnacles have much thicker, more robust shells than typical barnacles, and their bases are specially adapted with deep, penetrating roots that anchor firmly into whale skin. They also tend to be larger and more conical in shape compared to the flatter barnacles found on rocks.
children.funFact: Whale barnacles are so perfectly adapted to life on their hosts that they cannot survive anywhere else - if removed from a whale, they will quickly die, making them one of nature's most specialized hitchhikers.

children.description: Symmetrical Sessile Barnacles are marine crustaceans that permanently attach themselves to rocks, docks, boat hulls, and other hard surfaces. They live inside cone-shaped shells made of overlapping plates and feed by extending feathery appendages to filter tiny organisms from the water. These barnacles are found throughout New England's intertidal zones and shallow waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other barnacle groups, these species have symmetrical shell plates arranged in a circular pattern around their bodies. They are also completely sessile, meaning they cannot move once they've settled and cemented themselves to a surface as juveniles.
children.funFact: Barnacles are actually more closely related to shrimp and crabs than to mollusks like clams and mussels, despite living in similar hard shells!

children.name: Anomopoda
Daphniidae
Simocephalus
children.description: Simocephalus is a genus of small freshwater crustaceans called water fleas that belong to the cladoceran group. These tiny animals swim through ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams using their large, branched antennae like oars. They filter feed on algae, bacteria, and other microscopic particles from the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Simocephalus water fleas can be identified by their distinctive helmet-shaped head and relatively large size compared to other cladocerans. Their shell (carapace) often has serrated or spiny edges that help distinguish different species.
children.funFact: Like many water fleas, Simocephalus can reproduce without mating during favorable conditions, with females producing genetic clones of themselves to rapidly build up populations when food is abundant.

children.name: Daphnia
children.description: Water-fleas are tiny freshwater crustaceans that swim through ponds, lakes, and streams using their large, branched antennae like oars. These microscopic creatures have transparent bodies that allow you to see their internal organs, and they filter-feed on algae and bacteria floating in the water. Despite their common name, they're not actually fleas but are more closely related to crabs and lobsters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Water-fleas can be identified by their distinctive jerky swimming motion and their large, prominent eye that takes up much of their head. Their bodies are enclosed in a clear, shell-like carapace that opens and closes like a clamshell.
children.funFact: Water-fleas can reproduce without mating for most of the year, creating identical clones of themselves, but switch to sexual reproduction when conditions become stressful to create genetically diverse offspring that can survive harsh times.

children.name: Scapholeberis
children.description: Scapholeberis is a genus of tiny freshwater crustaceans known as water fleas that live in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. These microscopic animals are filter feeders that swim through the water column using their branched antennae, feeding on algae and organic particles. They belong to the group called cladocerans, which are important members of freshwater plankton communities.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Scapholeberis can be distinguished from other water fleas by their distinctive helmet-like head shape and their habit of swimming near the water surface. They also have a unique ability to use surface tension to hang upside down from the water's surface film.
children.funFact: Despite being barely visible to the naked eye, Scapholeberis can reproduce through parthenogenesis, meaning females can produce offspring without mating, allowing populations to boom rapidly when conditions are favorable.

children.description: Daphniidae is a family of tiny freshwater crustaceans commonly known as water fleas, though they're not actually fleas at all. These microscopic animals are characterized by their distinctive bean-shaped, translucent bodies enclosed in a hard shell called a carapace, and they swim through the water using large, branched antennae that act like oars.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family can be distinguished from other water fleas by their relatively large size, prominent swimming antennae, and the way their carapace completely encloses their body except for the head.
children.funFact: Despite being nearly invisible to the naked eye, water fleas are crucial to freshwater ecosystems and can reproduce so rapidly that a single female can produce hundreds of offspring in just a few weeks without even needing to mate.

children.name: Chydoridae
Acroperus
children.description: Acroperus is a genus of tiny freshwater crustaceans known as cladocerans or water fleas. These microscopic animals are filter feeders that swim through ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams using their large, branched antennae for propulsion. They play an important role in freshwater food webs, feeding on algae and bacteria while serving as food for fish and other aquatic animals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Acroperus are distinguished by their distinctively curved, sickle-shaped body outline and their preference for living among aquatic plants rather than swimming freely in open water. Their body shape is more laterally compressed and elongated compared to the more rounded water fleas in other genera.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'water fleas,' these creatures are actually more closely related to lobsters and crabs than to insects, and they can reproduce without mating through a process called parthenogenesis.

children.name: Picripleuroxus
children.description: Picripleuroxus is a small genus of microscopic marine copepods, tiny crustaceans that drift in the ocean as part of the zooplankton community. These diminutive creatures are characterized by their elongated body shape and specialized feeding appendages that help them capture even smaller organisms and organic particles from the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be distinguished from other copepods by their distinctive body proportions and the specific arrangement of their swimming legs and antennae.
children.funFact: Despite being barely visible to the naked eye, these tiny copepods play a crucial role in marine food webs, serving as a vital link between microscopic algae and larger marine animals like fish and whales.

children.description: Chydoridae is a family of tiny freshwater crustaceans known as water fleas that live in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. These microscopic animals have a distinctive bean-shaped or oval shell that protects their soft body, and they use their feathery antennae to swim through the water in a jerky, hopping motion. They feed by filtering algae, bacteria, and organic particles from the water around them.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Chydoridae can be distinguished from other water flea families by their compact, rounded shell and relatively short antennae. Unlike some of their relatives, they tend to stay closer to the bottom of water bodies and move in short, controlled hops rather than long swimming strokes.
children.funFact: Despite being barely visible to the naked eye, some chydorid water fleas can reproduce through parthenogenesis, meaning females can create genetic copies of themselves without needing to mate!

children.name: Eurycercidae
Eurycercus
children.description: Eurycercus is a genus of large water fleas that are among the biggest members of the cladoceran group of tiny freshwater crustaceans. These microscopic animals have a distinctive oval, flattened body enclosed in a transparent shell-like covering called a carapace, and they swim through ponds and lakes using their large, branched antennae like oars.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Eurycercus can be distinguished from other water fleas by their notably large size (up to 3mm long), their extremely long rostrum (beak-like projection), and their unique swimming style of gliding through the water rather than the typical jerky hopping motion of smaller water fleas.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'water fleas,' Eurycercus and other cladocerans are actually more closely related to lobsters and crabs than to any type of flea or insect.

children.description: Eurycercidae is a small family of water fleas, tiny freshwater crustaceans that swim through ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. These microscopic animals are filter feeders that play an important role in aquatic food webs, serving as food for fish and other aquatic creatures while helping to keep water clean by consuming algae and bacteria.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their unusually large, flattened body shape and distinctive swimming style compared to other water fleas. They have a more oval, compressed body form that sets them apart from the more typical rounded water flea shape.
