children.funFact: Despite being microscopic, Eurycercidae water fleas can reproduce without mating through a process called parthenogenesis, essentially creating clones of themselves when environmental conditions are favorable.

children.description: Anomopods are a diverse group of tiny freshwater crustaceans commonly known as water fleas, though they're not actually fleas at all. These microscopic animals are filter feeders that swim through ponds, lakes, and streams using their large, branched antennae like oars. They play a crucial role in aquatic food webs, feeding on algae and bacteria while serving as food for fish and other aquatic predators.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Anomopods have a distinctive folded shell-like structure called a carapace that covers most of their body, and they move primarily by rowing with their second pair of antennae. Unlike other water flea groups, they have specialized filtering appendages and a unique body plan optimized for suspension feeding.
children.funFact: Many anomopods can reproduce without mating through a process called parthenogenesis, creating clones of themselves when conditions are favorable, but switch to sexual reproduction when stressed or when winter approaches.

children.name: Cyclopoida
Cyclopidae
Macrocyclops
children.description: Macrocyclops is a genus of tiny freshwater copepods, which are microscopic crustaceans that swim through ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. These minuscule animals are important members of freshwater plankton communities, serving as both predators of even smaller organisms and food for fish and other aquatic creatures. Despite their small size, they play a crucial role in freshwater ecosystems throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Macrocyclops are characterized by their relatively large size compared to other copepods and their distinctive body shape with a clearly segmented appearance. They have long antennae and powerful swimming appendages that help them navigate through the water column.
children.funFact: These tiny crustaceans can live for several months and are so small that hundreds could fit on the head of a pin, yet they're fierce predators that hunt other microscopic animals in the plankton.

children.name: Acanthocyclops
children.description: Acanthocyclops is a genus of tiny freshwater copepods, which are microscopic crustaceans that live in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. These miniature animals are important members of freshwater plankton communities, swimming through the water using their feathery antennae and feeding on even smaller organisms like bacteria and algae.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Acanthocyclops copepods can be identified by their distinctive spiny projections on their body segments and antennae, which give them their name ('acantho' means spiny). They also have a characteristic egg sac arrangement where females carry their eggs in paired sacs attached to their abdomen.
children.funFact: Despite being less than 2 millimeters long, these tiny copepods are incredibly abundant and can number in the thousands per liter of pond water, making them one of the most numerous animals on Earth.

children.name: Diacyclops
children.description: Diacyclops is a genus of tiny freshwater copepods, which are small crustaceans that swim through lakes, ponds, and streams. These microscopic animals are important members of aquatic food webs, serving as both predators of even smaller organisms and prey for fish and other aquatic creatures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Diacyclops can be distinguished from other copepods by their specific body segmentation patterns and the structure of their swimming appendages called antennae.
children.funFact: Despite being barely visible to the naked eye, these tiny copepods are incredibly efficient swimmers that can dart through the water at speeds equivalent to a human swimming several hundred miles per hour!

children.name: Eucyclops
children.description: Eucyclops is a genus of tiny freshwater crustaceans called copepods that swim through lakes, ponds, and streams using their feather-like antennae as oars. These microscopic animals are important members of the zooplankton community, feeding on even smaller organisms like bacteria and algae while serving as food for fish and other aquatic creatures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Eucyclops can be identified by their distinctive egg sacs that females carry attached to their bodies, and their characteristic swimming pattern of short bursts followed by gliding motions.
children.funFact: Despite being only about 1-2 millimeters long, Eucyclops copepods can live for several months and play a crucial role in transferring energy from microscopic producers to larger animals in freshwater food webs.

children.name: Paracyclops
children.description: Paracyclops is a genus of tiny freshwater crustaceans called copepods that swim freely in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. These microscopic animals are important members of the zooplankton community, feeding on even smaller organisms like bacteria and algae. They play a crucial role in freshwater food webs as both predators of microorganisms and prey for fish and other aquatic animals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Paracyclops can be distinguished from other copepod genera by their specific body segmentation patterns and the structure of their swimming appendages called antennae. They have a distinctive egg sac arrangement and unique features in their mouthparts that help scientists identify them under a microscope.
children.funFact: Despite being barely visible to the naked eye, Paracyclops copepods are incredibly efficient swimmers that can dart through the water at speeds equivalent to a human swimming several hundred miles per hour!

children.description: Cyclopidae are tiny freshwater crustaceans known as cyclops copepods, named after the mythical one-eyed giant because they have a single prominent eye in the center of their head. These microscopic animals are common in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England, where they swim with jerky, hopping movements using their long antennae and swimming legs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cyclops copepods can be distinguished from other copepods by their single central eye and their characteristic swimming style of short, rapid bursts followed by gliding. They also have relatively long antennae compared to their body size and lack the elaborate feathery appendages seen in some marine copepods.
children.funFact: Despite being only about 1-3 millimeters long, cyclops copepods are fierce predators that hunt other microscopic animals, including mosquito larvae, making them important natural pest controllers in freshwater habitats.

children.description: Cyclopoid copepods are tiny crustaceans that swim through freshwater ponds, lakes, and streams using their feathery antennae and legs. These microscopic animals are important members of the zooplankton community, feeding on even smaller organisms like bacteria, algae, and organic particles. They play a crucial role in aquatic food webs, serving as food for fish, amphibians, and aquatic insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other copepods, cyclopoids have a distinctive pear-shaped body and relatively short antennae that don't extend much beyond their head. They also have a characteristic jerky, stop-and-go swimming pattern rather than the smooth gliding motion of other copepod groups.
children.funFact: Cyclopoid copepods get their name from the mythical Cyclops because they appear to have a single eye in the center of their head, though it's actually a compound structure made of multiple light-sensing cells.

children.name: Scalpellomorpha
Lepadidae
Lepas
children.description: Goose barnacles are fascinating marine crustaceans that live attached to floating objects like driftwood, ships, and even whales. Unlike the cone-shaped barnacles you see on rocks, these have a distinctive stalk (called a peduncle) topped with a shell made of several white or translucent plates. They filter tiny particles from the water using feathery appendages that extend from their shells.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Goose barnacles are easily recognized by their long, flexible stalk that connects them to their attachment surface, unlike acorn barnacles which sit directly on rocks. Their shells are flattened and made up of five main plates rather than the six or more plates found in most other barnacle groups.
children.funFact: These barnacles got their name from a medieval European belief that they were actually the eggs or larvae of geese, helping to explain where migratory birds came from before their breeding grounds were discovered.

children.name: Dosima
children.description: Dosima is a genus of unusual barnacles that live a completely free-floating lifestyle in the open ocean, unlike most barnacles that attach to rocks or other surfaces. These fascinating crustaceans create their own buoyant foam rafts that allow them to drift with ocean currents while filter-feeding from the water column.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical barnacles that cement themselves to hard surfaces, Dosima species are pelagic and maintain buoyancy through specialized foam structures they secrete themselves.
children.funFact: Buoy barnacles can form floating colonies of hundreds of individuals, creating what looks like white foam patches drifting across the ocean surface that can sometimes wash up on beaches after storms.

children.description: Goose barnacles are marine crustaceans that attach themselves to floating objects like driftwood, ships, and even whales using a flexible, muscular stalk. Unlike the cone-shaped acorn barnacles we see on rocks, these barnacles have a distinctive two-part body with a stalk (called a peduncle) and a shell-covered head region that contains the animal's feeding apparatus. They filter tiny organisms and particles from the water using feathery appendages called cirri.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The flexible stalk that connects them to their attachment surface sets goose barnacles apart from their sessile acorn barnacle relatives. This stalk allows them to sway with currents and waves while maintaining their grip on floating debris.
children.funFact: Goose barnacles got their common name from a medieval European belief that barnacle geese hatched from these sea creatures, which explained why no one had ever seen the geese's nesting grounds (which were actually in the remote Arctic).

children.description: Scalpellomorpha is an order of barnacles that includes the familiar goose barnacles, which are stalked crustaceans that attach themselves to floating objects, rocks, and other surfaces in marine environments. Unlike the cone-shaped acorn barnacles we often see on rocky shores, these barnacles have a flexible stalk (called a peduncle) that connects their feeding apparatus to their attachment point. They filter tiny food particles from the water using feathery appendages called cirri.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are distinguished from other barnacles by having a distinct stalk or peduncle that elevates their main body above the surface they're attached to. This gives them a distinctive goose-neck appearance, quite different from the low, volcano-like shape of acorn barnacles.
children.funFact: Goose barnacles got their common name from a medieval European belief that they were actually the eggs of barnacle geese, since people observed the geese arriving from unknown northern breeding grounds around the same time these stalked barnacles appeared on driftwood.

children.name: Anostraca
Chirocephalidae
Eubranchipus
children.description: Eubranchipus is a genus of fairy shrimp - tiny, translucent crustaceans that swim upside-down in temporary pools and ponds. These delicate creatures have elongated bodies with feathery swimming appendages and typically appear in early spring when snowmelt and rain fill shallow woodland pools. All members of this genus are found in cooler northern climates and depend on seasonal water bodies that dry up completely during summer.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Eubranchipus fairy shrimp can be distinguished from other fairy shrimp genera by their specific body proportions and the shape of their reproductive structures, particularly the males' specialized clasping organs called claspers.
children.funFact: These fairy shrimp can survive freezing temperatures as drought-resistant eggs that lie dormant in dried pond sediment for years, hatching only when conditions are just right in temporary spring pools.

children.description: Chirocephalidae is a family of fairy shrimp, tiny freshwater crustaceans that swim upside-down in temporary pools and ponds. These delicate, translucent creatures have elongated bodies with numerous paddle-like appendages that they use for both swimming and filter-feeding on algae and organic particles. They're specially adapted to life in seasonal wetlands that freeze in winter or dry up in summer.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family can be distinguished from other fairy shrimp by their distinctive head appendages and the specific structure of their reproductive organs. Males typically have elaborate, branched clasping organs that vary dramatically between species.
children.funFact: Fairy shrimp eggs can survive being completely dried out or frozen solid for years, hatching only when conditions are just right in their temporary aquatic homes.

children.description: Fairy shrimps are small, delicate freshwater crustaceans that swim upside-down through temporary pools and ponds using their feathery, leaf-like legs. These primitive shrimp-like creatures are most commonly found in seasonal wetlands, vernal pools, and other water bodies that dry up periodically. They play an important role in aquatic food webs as filter feeders that consume algae, bacteria, and organic particles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other small aquatic crustaceans, fairy shrimps lack a protective shell or carapace covering their segmented bodies, giving them a translucent, ethereal appearance. They also swim belly-up using rhythmic beating of their numerous paddle-like appendages, which is the opposite of most other swimming crustaceans.
children.funFact: Fairy shrimps have evolved to thrive in temporary pools by producing drought-resistant eggs that can survive completely dried out for years, hatching when the pools refill with water.

children.name: Stomatopoda
Squillidae
Squilla
children.description: Squilla is a genus of mantis shrimp, fascinating marine crustaceans that are actually neither mantises nor shrimp, but belong to their own unique group called stomatopods. These predators have powerful raptorial claws that they use to strike prey with incredible speed and force, earning them the nickname 'thumb splitters' among fishermen. They live in burrows in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms where they hunt for fish, crabs, and other marine creatures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of genus Squilla are distinguished from other mantis shrimp by their robust build, relatively large size, and their preference for burrowing in soft sediments rather than living in rock crevices.
children.funFact: Squilla mantis shrimp can punch with the force of a bullet, accelerating their club-like appendages at the same speed as a gunshot and creating cavitation bubbles that collapse with a secondary shockwave.

children.description: Squillid mantis shrimps are marine crustaceans known for their powerful raptorial claws that they use to strike prey with incredible force. These fascinating creatures have complex eyes with exceptional color vision and live in burrows they dig in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms. Despite their name, they are not true shrimp but belong to their own distinct group of crustaceans.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Squillids are distinguished from other mantis shrimp families by their robust body structure and particularly large, club-like striking appendages. They typically have broader, more heavily armored bodies compared to their spear-armed relatives.
children.funFact: A mantis shrimp's punch can accelerate faster than a bullet and create cavitation bubbles that collapse with a flash of light and temperatures nearly as hot as the sun's surface!

children.name: Nannosquillidae
Nannosquilla
children.description: Nannosquilla is a genus of small mantis shrimps, marine crustaceans known for their powerful raptorial claws used to capture prey. These compact predators live in burrows in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms, where they ambush small fish, worms, and other marine creatures. Despite their small size, they possess some of the most sophisticated eyes in the animal kingdom.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Nannosquilla species are among the smallest mantis shrimps, typically measuring less than 2 inches long. They have relatively shorter, more compact bodies compared to their larger mantis shrimp relatives, and their raptorial claws are proportionally smaller but still highly effective for their size.
children.funFact: Despite being tiny, Nannosquilla mantis shrimps can strike with their claws at speeds comparable to a bullet, creating cavitation bubbles in the water that collapse with a sharp popping sound.

children.description: Nannosquillidae is a family of small mantis shrimp that live in marine environments. These crustaceans are much smaller than their more famous mantis shrimp relatives, typically measuring just a few centimeters in length. They burrow in sandy or muddy seafloors and are active predators that catch small prey with their specialized raptorial claws.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished from other mantis shrimp by their small size and relatively simple body structure. They lack the elaborate eye stalks and powerful striking appendages that characterize larger mantis shrimp species.
children.funFact: Despite being tiny compared to their giant mantis shrimp cousins, nannosquillids still possess the lightning-fast reflexes that make mantis shrimp famous, using their quick strikes to capture prey in the blink of an eye.

children.name: Lysiosquillidae
Lysiosquilla
children.description: Lysiosquilla is a genus of mantis shrimps that are powerful marine predators found in coastal waters. These crustaceans are known for their impressive hunting abilities and distinctive body structure with large, raptorial front claws used to capture prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Lysiosquilla are characterized by their elongated bodies and particularly well-developed striking appendages that they use like clubs to stun fish and other prey.
children.funFact: Mantis shrimps in this genus can strike with the speed of a bullet, generating forces powerful enough to break through crab shells and even aquarium glass!

children.description: Banded mantis shrimps are marine crustaceans that belong to the stomatopod order, known for their powerful raptorial claws used to catch prey. Despite their name, they are neither mantises nor true shrimp, but rather unique predators that live in burrows in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms. These creatures have elongated bodies with distinctive banded patterns across their segments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their more famous club-wielding cousins, banded mantis shrimps are 'spearers' that use sharp, spike-like appendages to impale soft-bodied prey rather than smashing hard-shelled animals. They can be distinguished from other mantis shrimp families by their more slender build and preference for burrowing in softer substrates.
children.funFact: Banded mantis shrimps can strike with their spear-like claws at speeds comparable to a bullet, creating cavitation bubbles in the water that collapse with a loud snapping sound.

children.description: Mantis shrimps are fascinating marine crustaceans that are neither mantises nor shrimp, but rather occupy their own distinct order. These colorful predators are known for their incredibly powerful raptorial claws that can strike with the force of a bullet, and their remarkably complex eyes that can see polarized light and many more colors than humans can perceive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other crustaceans, mantis shrimps have large, prominent compound eyes on movable stalks and specialized front appendages that fold like a praying mantis. Their segmented bodies are typically flattened and they possess some of the most sophisticated visual systems in the animal kingdom.
children.funFact: Mantis shrimps have the most complex eyes in the animal kingdom, with up to 16 different types of color receptors (humans have only 3), allowing them to see ultraviolet, visible, and polarized light all at once.

children.name: Onychopoda
Polyphemidae
Polyphemus
children.description: Polyphemus is a genus containing a single species of freshwater crustacean known as the spiny water flea. These tiny zooplankton are actually not fleas at all, but rather members of the cladoceran group, which are small crustaceans that swim through the water column of lakes and ponds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Polyphemus is distinguished from other water fleas by its extremely long, barbed tail spine that can be up to four times longer than its body. Unlike most cladocerans, it has a relatively large eye and lacks the typical carapace that covers the body in related species.
children.funFact: The genus name Polyphemus comes from the one-eyed giant in Greek mythology, referring to the creature's single, prominent compound eye that takes up much of its transparent head.

children.description: Polyphemidae is a small family of freshwater water fleas that are among the largest members of the zooplankton community. These tiny crustaceans are predators that hunt other zooplankton using their large, prominent eyes and powerful swimming abilities. They play an important role in freshwater food webs as both predators of smaller zooplankton and prey for fish.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other water fleas, polyphemids have a distinctly large, single compound eye that takes up much of their head, giving them excellent vision for hunting prey. They also have long, branched antennae that they use like oars for rapid swimming.
children.funFact: The single species found in New England, Polyphemus pediculus, is named after the one-eyed giant Polyphemus from Greek mythology due to its massive, prominent eye that dominates its tiny head.

children.name: Cercopagididae
Bythotrephes
children.description: Bythotrephes is a genus of small aquatic crustaceans known as spiny waterfleas. These tiny predators live in freshwater lakes and have distinctive long, barbed tail spines that make up most of their body length. They are efficient hunters that feed on other small zooplankton in the water column.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The exceptionally long, sharp tail spine with barbs sets Bythotrephes apart from other waterfleas. This spine can be up to four times longer than the animal's actual body.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'waterfleas,' Bythotrephes are actually crustaceans more closely related to shrimp and crabs than to fleas, and their barbed tail spines often get tangled in fishing lines, helping them spread to new lakes.

children.description: Cercopagididae are tiny predatory water fleas that swim freely in freshwater lakes and ponds. These microscopic crustaceans are characterized by their distinctive long, spiny tail that can be longer than their body, which they use for protection and mobility.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other water fleas, cercopagids have an extremely long, barbed tail spine that makes up most of their total length. They are also active predators that hunt other zooplankton, rather than filter-feeding like many of their relatives.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Bythotrephes, is actually an invasive species from Europe that likely arrived in ship ballast water and has dramatically altered lake food webs by outcompeting native zooplankton.

children.name: Podonidae
Evadne
children.description: Evadne is a genus of tiny marine crustaceans called water fleas that drift through ocean waters as part of the zooplankton community. These microscopic animals have transparent, oval-shaped bodies and use their large antennae like oars to swim through the water column. They are filter feeders that consume even smaller plankton and organic particles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their freshwater cousins, Evadne species are marine water fleas with a distinctive brood pouch where females carry their developing eggs. They have a more streamlined, less rounded body shape compared to typical freshwater water fleas.
children.funFact: Despite being less than 2 millimeters long, Evadne can produce multiple generations in a single summer, with females capable of reproducing without mating through a process called parthenogenesis.

children.description: Podonidae are tiny marine crustaceans that live in the open ocean as part of the zooplankton community. These small water fleas are filter feeders that use their specialized appendages to capture even smaller organisms and particles from the water around them.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other water fleas, Podonidae have a distinctive body shape with a large head and a reduced, compact body that lacks the prominent shell covering found in their freshwater relatives.
children.funFact: Despite being nearly transparent and only a few millimeters long, these ocean drifters can reproduce both sexually and asexually, allowing them to rapidly increase their numbers when conditions are favorable.

children.description: Onychopoda are small freshwater crustaceans commonly known as water fleas that are distinguished by their large, prominent eyes and unique swimming style. These tiny aquatic animals are predators that actively hunt other small zooplankton, using their well-developed limbs to capture prey. They play an important role in freshwater ecosystems as both predators of smaller organisms and food sources for fish.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other water fleas, onychopods have greatly reduced swimming legs and instead use their large antennae for propulsion, giving them a distinctive jerky swimming motion. Their oversized compound eyes and predatory lifestyle also set them apart from their more common filter-feeding relatives.
children.funFact: Some onychopods can detect the chemical alarm signals released by their prey, allowing them to track down frightened zooplankton like tiny aquatic bloodhounds.

Attheyella
children.description: Attheyella is a genus of tiny freshwater copepods, which are microscopic crustaceans that live in lakes, ponds, and streams. These minuscule animals are important members of freshwater plankton communities, swimming through the water column using their feathery appendages. They play a crucial role in aquatic food webs as both predators of even smaller organisms and prey for fish and other aquatic creatures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Attheyella can be distinguished from other copepod genera by their specific body segmentation patterns and the arrangement of setae (bristle-like structures) on their appendages. They typically have a more elongated body shape compared to some of their close relatives.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, a single Attheyella copepod can consume hundreds of bacteria and algae cells per day, making them tiny but mighty water purifiers in freshwater ecosystems.

children.name: Canthocamptus
children.description: Canthocamptus is a genus of tiny freshwater copepods, microscopic crustaceans that swim through ponds, lakes, and streams. These minuscule animals are important members of aquatic ecosystems, feeding on algae, bacteria, and organic particles while serving as food for fish and other aquatic creatures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their elongated body shape and distinctive swimming antennae. They can be distinguished from other copepod genera by their specific body segmentation patterns and the structure of their swimming appendages.
children.funFact: Despite being barely visible to the naked eye, these tiny copepods are incredibly abundant and can number in the thousands per liter of pond water, making them one of the most numerous animals in freshwater habitats.

children.name: Bryocamptus
children.description: Bryocamptus is a genus of tiny freshwater copepods, which are microscopic crustaceans that swim through ponds, streams, and other aquatic habitats. These minute animals are part of the zooplankton community and play important roles in freshwater food webs as both predators of even smaller organisms and prey for fish and other aquatic creatures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their specific body segmentation patterns and the structure of their swimming appendages (antennae and legs). They have characteristic features in their reproductive structures that separate them from other copepod genera.
children.funFact: Despite being nearly invisible to the naked eye, these tiny copepods are incredibly abundant in freshwater systems and can be among the most numerous animals in a pond or stream.

children.description: Canthocamptidae is a family of tiny freshwater copepods, microscopic crustaceans that live in lakes, ponds, streams, and even wet moss and leaf litter. These minuscule animals are incredibly abundant and play crucial roles as both predators of bacteria and algae, and as food for larger aquatic creatures. Despite their small size, they're skilled swimmers that use their antennae and legs to navigate through water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their elongated, worm-like body shape and relatively long antennae compared to other copepod families. They typically have a more flexible body structure that helps them navigate through tight spaces in sediment and vegetation.
children.funFact: Some Canthocamptidae copepods can survive completely drying out by entering a dormant state, allowing them to live in temporary puddles and even the thin water films around moss and soil particles.

children.description: Harpacticoid copepods are tiny crustaceans that live primarily on or near the bottom of aquatic environments, crawling and swimming through sediments, algae, and plant matter. Unlike their free-swimming relatives, these microscopic animals prefer to stay close to surfaces where they can graze on bacteria, algae, and organic particles. They're found in both freshwater and marine environments throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Harpacticoid copepods are distinguished from other copepods by their bottom-dwelling lifestyle and shorter, more robust body shape adapted for crawling rather than swimming. They typically have a more flattened body and stronger legs compared to the streamlined, free-swimming copepods.
children.funFact: Despite being less than a millimeter long, harpacticoid copepods are ecological powerhouses that help recycle nutrients by breaking down dead organic matter in aquatic sediments.

children.name: Mysida
Mysidae
Praunus
children.description: Praunus is a genus of small, translucent marine shrimp that live in coastal waters and estuaries. These delicate crustaceans are excellent swimmers that feed on tiny plankton and organic particles in the water column.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Praunus shrimp are characterized by their transparent bodies and ability to rapidly change color for camouflage, earning them the common name 'chameleon shrimp.'
children.funFact: Despite being called 'chameleon shrimp,' these creatures can change color much faster than actual chameleons, shifting from transparent to brown or green in just seconds to match their surroundings.

children.name: Mysis
children.description: Mysis is a genus of small, shrimp-like crustaceans known as mysid shrimp or opossum shrimp. These translucent creatures live in cold freshwater lakes and are important members of aquatic food webs, serving as prey for fish while feeding on plankton and organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mysis can be distinguished from true shrimp by their unique brood pouch where females carry their eggs and young, earning them the nickname 'opossum shrimp.' They also have a distinctive swimming style, moving both forward and backward with equal ease using their pleopods.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'shrimp,' Mysis are actually more closely related to krill and have a fascinating life history where the young develop completely inside their mother's brood pouch before being released as miniature adults.

children.description: Mysidae, commonly known as opossum shrimp or mysid shrimp, are small translucent crustaceans that live in both marine and freshwater environments. Despite their common name, they are not true shrimp but belong to their own distinct group of shrimplike creatures. These delicate animals are typically less than an inch long and swim in large swarms near the water's surface or bottom.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mysids can be distinguished from true shrimp by their thin, almost transparent bodies and the presence of a special brood pouch (marsupium) where females carry their developing young. Unlike shrimp, they also have statocysts - small organs that help them maintain balance and orientation in the water.
children.funFact: Mysids are called 'opossum shrimp' because females carry their babies in a pouch just like opossums, making them one of the few crustaceans with this marsupial-like trait.

children.description: Opossum shrimps are small, translucent marine crustaceans that swim in coastal waters and estuaries. Despite their name, they're not true shrimp but belong to their own distinct group of animals that carry their young in a pouch, much like opossums do on land.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true shrimp, opossum shrimps have a special brood pouch where females carry their developing eggs and young. They also have distinctive statocysts (balance organs) in their tail fan that help them orient themselves in the water.
children.funFact: Opossum shrimps can live for over a year and migrate vertically in the water column daily, rising toward the surface at night to feed and sinking deeper during the day to avoid predators.

children.name: Calanoida
Diaptomidae
Aglaodiaptomus
children.description: Aglaodiaptomus is a genus of freshwater copepods, tiny crustaceans that swim freely in lakes and ponds throughout New England. These microscopic animals are important members of the zooplankton community, feeding on algae and other small organisms while serving as food for fish and other aquatic creatures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by their distinctive body shape and specialized swimming appendages called antennae that help them move through the water in a characteristic jerky, hopping motion.
children.funFact: Despite being less than 2 millimeters long, these tiny copepods are considered keystone species in freshwater ecosystems because they help control algae populations and transfer energy up the food chain to larger animals.

children.description: Diaptomidae is a family of freshwater copepods, which are tiny crustaceans that swim freely in lakes, ponds, and streams. These microscopic animals are important members of the zooplankton community, serving as a crucial link in aquatic food webs by feeding on algae and bacteria while being eaten by fish and other aquatic creatures. They have elongated, torpedo-shaped bodies with long antennae that they use for swimming and sensing their environment.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Diaptomid copepods can be distinguished from other copepod families by their characteristic body shape with a distinct separation between the head and thorax, and their particularly long first antennae. The males often have modified antennae that are used for grasping females during mating.
children.funFact: Some diaptomid copepods can produce resting eggs that can survive for decades in dried-up pond sediments, hatching when water returns to create an instant population.

children.name: Clausocalanidae
Pseudocalanus
children.description: Pseudocalanus is a genus of small marine copepods that are among the most abundant zooplankton in cold ocean waters. These tiny crustaceans are crucial components of marine food webs, serving as primary grazers of phytoplankton and as essential food sources for fish, whales, and other marine animals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Pseudocalanus are distinguished from other copepod genera by their elongated body shape and specific arrangement of swimming appendages. They have a distinctive oval-shaped body with long antennules that extend beyond their body length.
children.funFact: Despite being barely visible to the naked eye at only 1-2 millimeters long, Pseudocalanus copepods can migrate hundreds of feet vertically in the water column each day, rising to surface waters at night to feed and descending to deeper waters during the day.

children.description: Clausocalanidae is a family of small marine copepods, which are tiny crustaceans that drift in ocean waters as part of the zooplankton community. These microscopic animals are important members of marine food webs, serving as food for fish, whales, and other marine creatures. They swim through the water column using their feathery appendages and feed on even smaller organisms like phytoplankton.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their compact body shape and specific arrangements of swimming legs and sensory structures. They can be distinguished from other copepod families by their unique combination of antenna structure and the way their body segments are organized.
children.funFact: Despite being barely visible to the naked eye, these tiny copepods can perform daily vertical migrations of hundreds of feet, swimming toward the surface at night to feed and returning to deeper waters during the day to avoid predators.

children.description: Calanoid copepods are tiny aquatic crustaceans that are among the most abundant animals on Earth, living in both freshwater and marine environments. These microscopic creatures are characterized by their elongated, streamlined bodies and long antennae that they use for swimming and feeding. They play a crucial role in aquatic food webs as both filter feeders that consume algae and bacteria, and as food for fish and other larger animals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Calanoid copepods can be distinguished from other copepods by their long, straight antennae and their swimming style - they move through the water in a jerky, stop-and-go motion rather than smoothly gliding.
children.funFact: Some calanoid copepods perform daily vertical migrations that can span hundreds of feet, swimming up to surface waters at night to feed and diving deep during the day to avoid predators - one of the largest animal migrations on the planet by distance relative to body size.

children.description: Meganyctiphanes is a genus of large krill, which are small shrimp-like marine crustaceans that live in the ocean. These creatures are filter feeders that swim in large swarms and form a crucial part of the marine food web, serving as food for whales, fish, and seabirds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Meganyctiphanes krill are notably larger than most other krill species and have distinctive bioluminescent organs called photophores that allow them to produce their own light.
children.funFact: Northern krill can live up to 6 years, which is exceptionally long for krill species, and they perform daily vertical migrations, swimming to surface waters at night to feed and returning to deeper waters during the day.

children.description: Euphotic krill are small, shrimp-like marine crustaceans that live in the sunlit upper layers of the ocean. These translucent creatures are powerful swimmers with large compound eyes and long antennae, spending their lives drifting and swimming in massive swarms throughout the world's oceans.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true shrimp, krill have their gills exposed outside their body rather than hidden under a shell-like covering. They also have distinctive light-producing organs called photophores that create a bioluminescent glow.
children.funFact: Despite being only a few inches long, krill form some of the largest animal aggregations on Earth, with swarms sometimes containing millions of individuals and stretching for miles across the ocean surface.

children.description: Krill are small, shrimp-like marine crustaceans that swim in the open ocean. They have transparent bodies with large black eyes and feed primarily on tiny floating plants and animals called plankton. These creatures form massive swarms that can contain millions of individuals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true shrimp, krill have external gills that look like feathery plates and their legs are more visible from the outside. They also have light-producing organs called photophores that can create bioluminescent displays.
children.funFact: Despite their small size, krill are considered one of the most important species on Earth because they form the base of many ocean food webs, feeding everything from small fish to the largest whales.

children.description: Limnadiidae are small freshwater crustaceans known as clam shrimp that live in temporary pools, ponds, and wetlands. They have a bivalved shell that looks like a tiny clam, but they're actually more closely related to fairy shrimp and other branchiopods. These creatures are filter feeders that swim through the water using their leaf-like legs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other clam shrimp families, Limnadiidae have a distinctive rounded shell shape and specific arrangements of growth lines on their carapace. They also have unique reproductive strategies, with some species capable of both sexual and asexual reproduction.
children.funFact: Some clam shrimp in this family are hermaphrodites that can fertilize their own eggs, allowing a single individual to colonize a new habitat and establish an entire population.

children.description: Spinicaudata are small freshwater crustaceans commonly known as clam shrimp because of their bivalved shell that resembles a tiny clam. These ancient creatures swim and crawl through temporary pools, ponds, and wetlands using their many pairs of leaf-like swimming legs. They are filter feeders that strain tiny particles of food from the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their relatives the fairy shrimp, clam shrimp are enclosed in a hinged, clam-like shell that can completely protect their body. They also have more pairs of swimming legs than most other branchiopods.
children.funFact: Clam shrimp are living fossils that have remained virtually unchanged for over 400 million years, making them older than the dinosaurs!

children.funFact: Clam shrimp can survive in temporary pools that dry up completely by producing drought-resistant eggs that can remain dormant in dried mud for years until water returns.

children.description: Laevicaudata are tiny freshwater crustaceans that live in temporary pools, ponds, and wetlands. These small creatures are clam shrimp, meaning they have a bivalved shell that can completely enclose their body, much like a tiny clam. They are filter feeders that swim through the water using their leaf-like legs to capture microscopic food particles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other clam shrimp, Laevicaudata have a smooth, unmarked shell without growth lines or ridges. Their shell also lacks the distinctive umbo (raised bump) found in related groups.
children.funFact: These ancient creatures can survive drought by producing eggs that remain dormant in dried mud for years, then hatch when water returns to their habitat.

children.description: Derocheilocaris is a genus of tiny marine crustaceans that belong to the mysterious group called mystacocarids. These microscopic animals live in the spaces between sand grains in coastal areas, where they crawl through the wet sediment using their specialized appendages. They represent one of the most primitive groups of crustaceans still alive today.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other small crustaceans, Derocheilocaris has a unique combination of primitive features including a segmented body with simple appendages and lacks the specialized swimming structures found in copepods or the complex mouthparts of other crustacean groups.
children.funFact: Derocheilocaris was only discovered in 1943 and is so rare and small (less than 0.5mm long) that scientists initially thought it might be a larval stage of another animal rather than a distinct adult crustacean.

children.description: Derocheilocarididae is a family of extremely small marine crustaceans that live in the spaces between sand grains on ocean floors. These microscopic animals are part of an ancient group called mystacocarids, which are considered living fossils that have remained virtually unchanged for millions of years.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their primitive body structure with a simple, elongated form and lack the complex appendages found in most other crustaceans. They have a unique combination of features that place them as one of the most basal groups within the crustacean family tree.
children.funFact: Despite being discovered relatively recently in 1943, these tiny creatures represent one of the oldest lineages of crustaceans and provide scientists with a window into what early crustacean ancestors may have looked like over 400 million years ago.

children.description: Mystacocarids are tiny marine crustaceans that live in the spaces between sand grains on beaches and in shallow coastal waters. These microscopic animals are among the smallest known crustaceans, typically measuring less than half a millimeter in length. They crawl through the interstitial spaces of sandy sediments, feeding on organic matter and bacteria.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mystacocarids are distinguished by their extremely small size, elongated worm-like body shape, and reduced number of body segments compared to other crustaceans. They lack eyes and have simplified appendages adapted for their life in tight spaces between sand grains.
children.funFact: Mystacocarids were only discovered in 1943 and are considered living fossils, representing one of the most primitive groups of crustaceans with features that may resemble the earliest crustacean ancestors from hundreds of millions of years ago.
